spacetimes.name: Black String
spacetimes.description: Schwarzschild's black hole extended along one more direction of space, a static vacuum solution of gravity in five or more dimensions whose horizon is a cylinder. Ruth Gregory and Raymond Laflamme showed in 1993 that ripples along it longer than about seven horizon radii grow, and numerical evolutions of that instability end in a naked singularity.
spacetimes.convention: The horizon radius is fixed by the string's mass per unit length, $M/L$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.

related.text: The black string is Schwarzschild's black hole at every point of a line. Every slice of constant $z$ is Schwarzschild's spacetime [gregory2012].

The other way to carry Schwarzschild's black hole into five dimensions, with a round horizon, a 3-sphere. It has more entropy than a long enough piece of string of the same mass [gregorylaflamme1993].

Another vacuum solution of five dimensions with one direction rolled into a circle. Seen from four dimensions the string is Schwarzschild's black hole and the monopole is a magnetic charge [gregory2012, grossperry1983].
A wall in anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions, on which Schwarzschild's black hole is a black string that reaches away from the wall into the fifth [chamblin2000].
The black string with its extra direction a circle, set moving around it. Seen from four dimensions the moving string is an electrically charged black hole [horowitz2012].
A black ring in orbit around a black hole. Where the ring is thin it is a black string bent into a circle, and it is expected to ripple as the string does [elvang2006, elvang2007].

charts.name: Schwarzschild

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/(c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi, z)$, Schwarzschild's with the length $z$ along the string added, and $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/(c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi, z)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ a length and $z$ the length along the string.

charts.name: Kerr-Schild

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/(c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(T, r, \theta, \phi, z)$, with the time $T = (v - r)/c = t + (r_s/c)\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ of the ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein chart carrying dimensions of time and $z$ the length along the string. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Schwarzschild, Six Dimensions

parameters.description: Horizon radius, $r_h^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2L)$ for a length $L$ of string of mass $M$, with $G$ Newton's constant in six dimensions

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \psi, \theta, \phi, z)$ in $D = 6$, the static chart of the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini black hole of five dimensions with the length $z$ along the string added, and $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Bonnor Beam of Light
spacetimes.description: The exact gravitational field of a steady beam of light, which William Bonnor found in 1969, a plane-fronted gravitational wave that keeps pace with the light. A ray moving with the beam feels nothing, a ray moving against it is drawn in, and two beams shining the same way do not attract each other.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $G$ and $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: The whole family of plane-fronted waves with parallel rays. Bonnor's beam is the member whose profile holds still in time and has light for its source [bonnor1969light].

A pulse of light with no width and no length, the field of one massless particle. Bonnor wrote its profile down in 1969 as the sharpest pulse, and Aichelburg and Sexl reached it in 1971 by boosting Schwarzschild's field [bonnor1969light, aichelburg1971].
The static vacuum outside a line of matter. Two beams shining in opposite directions make a static source, and Dietrich Kramer joined their exact field to Levi-Civita's metric in 1998 [kramer1998].
Another of Bonnor's electromagnetic spacetimes, a bundle of magnetic field lines held together by its own gravity. He found it in 1954, ten years before Melvin [bonnor1954].
The beam switched off. With $A = 0$ the metric is Minkowski's, and on the axis of a uniform beam the plane of $t$ and $z$ is flat with the light still on.
Light as the source again, here streaming out of a point mass and pushing it along. Bonnor named its rectilinear case the photon rocket in 1994 [bonnor1994].
Light as the source again, here streaming out of a star evenly in all directions. Prahlad Vaidya found the field around the star in 1951 [vaidya1951].

charts.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Profile of the beams, a dimensionless function of the two transverse coordinates, with $A \ge 0$. The energy density of the light is $\epsilon = c^4\left(\partial_x^2 A + \partial_y^2 A\right)/16\pi G$, so $A$ is harmonic outside the beams

charts.convention: We use William Bonnor's coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and the beams shining toward $+z$, in the signature $(-,+,+,+)$, where his profile $A \ge 0$ enters with a minus sign. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 - A\left(c\,dt - dz\right)^2

charts.name: Null Cartesian

parameters.description: Profile of the beams, a dimensionless function of the two transverse coordinates, with $A \ge 0$. The energy density of the light is $\epsilon = c^4\left(\partial_x^2 A + \partial_y^2 A\right)/16\pi G$, so $A$ is harmonic outside the beams

charts.convention: We use William Bonnor's null coordinates $\sqrt{2}\,u = ct - z$ and $\sqrt{2}\,v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $x$ and $y$ the transverse lengths and the beams shining along the rays of constant $u$, $x$, and $y$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Null Cylindrical, Inside the Beam

parameters.description: Newton's gravitational constant
Energy density of the light, uniform across the beam; the energy per unit length of the beam is $\pi R^2\epsilon$
Radius of the beam

charts.convention: We use William Bonnor's null coordinates $\sqrt{2}\,u = ct - z$ and $\sqrt{2}\,v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $\rho$ the distance from the axis of the beam and $\phi$ the angle about it. The light has the uniform energy density $\epsilon$ out to the radius $R$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Null Cylindrical, Outside the Beam

parameters.description: Newton's gravitational constant
Energy density of the light, uniform across the beam; the energy per unit length of the beam is $\pi R^2\epsilon$
Radius of the beam

charts.convention: We use William Bonnor's null coordinates $\sqrt{2}\,u = ct - z$ and $\sqrt{2}\,v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $\rho$ the distance from the axis of the beam and $\phi$ the angle about it. The beam, of energy density $\epsilon$, fills $\rho \le R$, and the metric and its first derivatives are continuous at its edge. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

spacetimes.name: Bonnor's Magnetic Dipole
spacetimes.description: The static field of a mass with a magnetic dipole moment, the solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations William Bonnor found in 1966. Roberto Emparan showed in 2000 that its two poles are extremal black holes with opposite magnetic charges, held apart by a strut on the axis between them.
spacetimes.convention: The parameter $m$ is a length, and the mass $M$ has $GM/c^2 = 2m$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: The dipole with $b = 0$, which is Zipoy and Voorhees's deformed mass at $q = 1$: a mass with a quadrupole and no magnet [emparan2000].

The spinning black hole Bonnor's rule starts from. The rule trades Kerr's twist for a magnetic potential, and the dipole keeps Kerr's two functions with $a^2$ turned into $-b^2$ [bonnor2002, davidson1994].
Each pole on its own. In the limit $b \to \infty$ the poles are infinitely far apart, and the neighbourhood of each is an extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole [emparan2000].
Extremal black holes with charges of one sign, which balance with no strut. Give two of them opposite charges and both forces pull, which is Bonnor's dipole [emparan2000].
The magnetic universe, which Bonnor found in 1954. Set in its field by a Harrison transformation, the dipole loses its strut at one field strength [bonnor1954, emparan2000].
The throat of an extremal charged black hole. Each pole of the dipole opens into such a throat, and with the pair balanced by an outside field it is exactly Bertotti and Robinson's [emparan2000].
Two black holes that accelerate apart. The dipole is the same pair at rest, and Emparan placed it on top of the barrier under which a magnetic field creates the accelerating pair [emparan2000].
A mass with no multipole beyond the monopole. The dipole with $b = 0$ keeps a quadrupole and a naked singularity, so it is not Schwarzschild's black hole [emparan2000].
The Weyl field of a point mass. In Weyl's coordinates each black hole of the dipole is a single point of the axis as well [emparanteo2001].
Gross and Perry's monopole of Kaluza-Klein theory. Their monopole and antimonopole pair is the dipole's counterpart in that theory [grossperry1983, emparan2000].

charts.name: Bonnor
domains: Z = 0 \;\text{(the axis between the black holes, with the strut)}

parameters.description: Half the mass as a length: the mass $M$ at spatial infinity has $GM/c^2 = 2m$
Dipole length, $b > 0$: the magnetic dipole moment is $2mb$ in units with $G = c = 1$, and the two black holes carry the magnetic charges $\pm m\left(m + \sqrt{m^2 + b^2}\right)/b$
Bonnor's first polynomial, an area, equal to $Z + b^2\sin^2\theta$; the magnetic potential is $A_\phi = 2mbr\sin^2\theta/P$ in units with $G = c = 1$
Bonnor's second polynomial, an area, equal to $Z + \left(m^2 + b^2\right)\sin^2\theta$
Bonnor's third polynomial, an area, equal to $P + 2mr$
Bonnor's fourth polynomial, an area, which vanishes at $r = m + \sqrt{m^2 + b^2}$, the axis between the two black holes

charts.convention: We use Bonnor's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length, in which Weyl's canonical coordinates are $\rho = \sqrt{Z}\sin\theta$ and $z = (r - m)\cos\theta$, and write $P$, $Q$, $Y$, and $Z$ for his four polynomials in $r$ and $\cos\theta$. The length $b$ is the ratio of the magnetic dipole moment to the mass. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Bonnor's Rotating Dust Cloud
spacetimes.description: A stationary, axially symmetric cloud of dust in rigid rotation that thins out to nothing in every direction, found by William Bonnor in 1977. Its total mass is zero, its centre is a singularity of negative mass, and the circles about the axis inside a torus around the centre are closed timelike curves.
spacetimes.convention: The length $a$ sets the rotation, with $a^2 = 2h$ for Bonnor's parameter $h$ and angular momentum $J = c^3a^2/2G$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: Lanczos and van Stockum's cylinder belongs to the same class of rigidly rotating dust, with a twist that grows as the square of the distance from the axis where Bonnor's is a dipole's. The cylinder runs on along its axis without end, and Bonnor's cloud thins out in every direction [vanstockum1937, bratek2007].
The cloud with its rotation switched off, $a = 0$, where the density vanishes and the line element is flat space in cylindrical coordinates [astesiano2024].

Kurt Gödel's universe of 1949, rigidly rotating dust with a cosmological constant and one density everywhere. Its closed timelike curves pass through every event, and Bonnor's cloud keeps its own inside a torus about the centre [godel1949, astesiano2024].
Far from its centre Bonnor's cloud has the frame dragging term of Kerr's metric, for an angular momentum $J = c^3a^2/2G$, and no mass term to go with it [bratek2007].

A static vacuum field built on the potential of a point, as Bonnor's cloud is in van Stockum's class. Each has a singularity at the origin whose strength depends on the direction of approach [gautreau1967, ilyas2017, astesiano2024].

charts.name: Cylindrical
domains: r^3 = a^2\rho \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, \rho, z \text{ are null)}
r^3 < a^2\rho \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, \rho, z \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Rotation length, $a^2 = 2h = 2GJ/c^3$ with $h$ Bonnor's rotation parameter and $J$ the angular momentum at spatial infinity; the circle of constant $t$ in the equatorial plane is null at a distance $a$ from the centre
Distance from the centre in the flat space of the coordinates; the twist of the dust is $a^2\rho^2/r^3$, a dipole's, and its density is $c^2/8\pi G$ times the Ricci scalar

charts.convention: We use the comoving cylindrical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$ of van Stockum's class, in which the dust is at rest, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, in the letters of Bratek, Jałocha, and Kutschera: Bonnor writes $r$ for our $\rho$ and $R$ for our $r = \sqrt{\rho^2 + z^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Spherical
domains: r^2 = a^2\sin\theta \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, r, \theta \text{ are null)}
r^2 < a^2\sin\theta \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, r, \theta \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Rotation length, $a^2 = 2h = 2GJ/c^3$ with $h$ Bonnor's rotation parameter and $J$ the angular momentum at spatial infinity; the circle of constant $t$ in the equatorial plane is null at a distance $a$ from the centre; the density of the dust is $c^2/8\pi G$ times the Ricci scalar

charts.convention: We use the spherical coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Bratek, Jałocha, and Kutschera, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, in which the dust is at rest and the cylindrical chart's $\rho = r\sin\theta$ and $z = r\cos\theta$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Bonnor-Vaidya Charged Radiating Star
spacetimes.description: Vaidya's radiating star with a charge: the field of a spherical body that sends out, or takes in, null dust carrying electric charge as well as energy, found by William Bonnor and Prahlad Vaidya in 1970 as an exact solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations. Its mass and its charge are functions of a null time, and where both are constant it is the charged black hole of Reissner and Nordström.
spacetimes.convention: We work in units with $c = 1$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: The same star with no charge to shed. With $q = 0$ the metric is Vaidya's [vaidya1951].
The charged black hole that neither gains nor loses. With $m$ and $q$ constant the metric is Reissner-Nordström's in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, with $r_s = 2m$ and $r_q = q$ [ori1991charged].
No charge and a constant mass. The metric is then Schwarzschild's in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, with $r_s = 2m$.
The same metric with the charge held constant, read inside a black hole. With a second stream of light running outward there, the mass function grows without limit at the inner horizon [poisson1989].

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein
domains: r\,\partial_u m = q\,\partial_u q \;\text{(where the energy density of the null dust changes sign)}

parameters.description: Mass inside the sphere of radius $r$ at the retarded time $u$, a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Charge inside that sphere, a length, $q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(u)$ and the charge $q(u)$ are functions of $u$ alone, both lengths. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein
domains: r\,\partial_v m = q\,\partial_v q \;\text{(where the energy density of the null dust changes sign)}

parameters.description: Mass inside the sphere of radius $r$ at the advanced time $v$, a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Charge inside that sphere, a length, $q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(v)$ and the charge $q(v)$ are functions of $v$ alone, both lengths. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Homothetic
domains: V \to -\infty \;\text{(the first ray, }v = 0\text{, flat space before it)}
2\mu R^3 - MR^2 + 2M^2R - MQ^2 = 0 \;\text{(the rays that keep their }R\text{)}
R = Q^2/M \;\text{(where the energy density of the null dust changes sign)}

parameters.description: Mass scale, a length: the mass is $m = Me^{\mu V/M}$, which grows as $\mu v$ in the advanced time $v = (M/\mu)e^{\mu V/M}$
Charge scale, a length: the charge is $q = Qe^{\mu V/M}$, in proportion to the mass
Rate $dm/dv$ at which the mass grows, a pure number

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(V, R, \theta, \phi)$, both lengths, for the mass and the charge that grow in proportion to the advanced time $v$: $V$ is its logarithm, $v = (M/\mu)e^{\mu V/M}$, and $R = rM/m$ is the areal radius $r$ in units of the mass $m = \mu v$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

spacetimes.name: Boson Stars and Geons
spacetimes.description: A ball of scalar field held together by its own gravity, the heir of John Wheeler's geon of light, found by David Kaup in 1968 and by Remo Ruffini and Silvano Bonazzola in 1969. The field turns in phase at a frequency $\omega$ while the spacetime stays static, with a regular centre and no horizon. The metric is known only numerically, as a solution of the Einstein-Klein-Gordon equations integrated outward from the centre, and the heaviest star has $M = 0.633\,M_P^2/m$ for bosons of mass $m$, with $M_P$ the Planck mass.
spacetimes.convention: We write the field of the star as $\varphi = \varphi_0(r)e^{i\omega t}$ for bosons of mass $m$, with $\mu = mc/\hbar$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{4\pi G}\,\varphi_0/c^2$ its dimensionless amplitude. We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.

related.text: The same balance for a star of fluid, where pressure does the holding up. Ruffini and Bonazzola put fermions through their method as well, and it "confirms the Oppenheimer-Volkoff treatment in extremely good approximation" [ruffini1969].

The star with no field in it: at $\sigma = 0$ the equations give $\alpha^2 = a^{-2} = 1 - r_s/r$. Far from a boson star the field has died away and the metric is Schwarzschild's for the star's mass [liebling2023].
The scalar field with no mass, at rest, which ends in a naked singularity at its centre [janis1968]. A boson star's field has a mass and a turning phase, and its centre is regular [liebling2023].
Mael Melvin's magnetic geon, parallel lines of magnetic field held together by their own gravity, Wheeler's idea in a cylinder [melvin1964].
A star held up by sideways stress alone, with none along its radius [einstein1939]. A boson star's two stresses differ as well, and neither star has an equation of state [ruffini1969].
Another star with no horizon offered as a stand in for a black hole, a ball of de Sitter space under a thin shell [mazur2004].

A ball of Yang-Mills field held together by its own gravity, also known only numerically. It comes as a ladder of solitons counted by the zeros of the field, and every one of them is unstable [bartnik1988, volkov1999].

Wheeler's geometrodynamics had a second way to get mass with no matter, the wormhole. Charles Misner's slice of 1960 has two masses at rest that are the two mouths of one wormhole in empty space [misner1957, misner1960].

charts.name: Polar Areal

parameters.description: Lapse, dimensionless: a clock held at radius $r$ runs at $\alpha$ of the rate $t$ counts. For the star it is known only numerically, as the solution of $\partial_r\alpha = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}\left[\dfrac{a^2 - 1}{r} + r\left(\left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{c^2\alpha^2} - \mu^2\right)a^2\sigma^2 + \left(\partial_r\sigma\right)^2\right)\right]$ that approaches $1$ far from the star

Radial function, dimensionless: $a\,dr$ is the proper distance along the radius, and $M(r) = c^2r\left(1 - a^{-2}\right)/2G$ is the mass inside the sphere of radius $r$. For the star it is known only numerically, as the solution of $\partial_r a = \dfrac{a}{2}\left[-\dfrac{a^2 - 1}{r} + r\left(\left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{c^2\alpha^2} + \mu^2\right)a^2\sigma^2 + \left(\partial_r\sigma\right)^2\right)\right]$ with $a(0) = 1$, where the field obeys $\partial_r^2\sigma = -\left(1 + a^2 - \mu^2r^2a^2\sigma^2\right)\dfrac{\partial_r\sigma}{r} - \left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{c^2\alpha^2} - \mu^2\right)a^2\sigma$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ that Liebling and Palenzuela call polar areal, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The lapse $\alpha(r)$ and the radial function $a(r)$ are dimensionless, and we leave both free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Isotropic

parameters.description: Lapse, dimensionless, the same function of the sphere as in the polar areal chart: a clock held at radius $R$ runs at $\alpha$ of the rate $t$ counts, and $\alpha$ approaches $1$ far from the star

Conformal factor, dimensionless: the areal radius is $r = \psi^2R$, and the radial function of the polar areal chart is $a = \psi/\left(\psi + 2R\,\partial_R\psi\right)$. For the star it is known only numerically, from $dR/dr = aR/r$, and far from the star it approaches $1 + GM/(2c^2R)$, with $M$ the mass of the star

charts.convention: We use Liebling and Palenzuela's isotropic coordinates $(t, R, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $R$ the isotropic radius, a length, so the areal radius is $r = \psi^2R$. The lapse $\alpha(R)$ and the conformal factor $\psi(R)$ are dimensionless, and we leave both free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Boulware-Deser Black Hole
spacetimes.description: The spherical black hole of Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity in five dimensions, which David Boulware and Stanley Deser found in 1985. The curvature squared term of string theory keeps its metric function finite at the centre and leaves a small mass with no horizon, and the same field equations have a second solution that approaches anti-de Sitter space.
spacetimes.convention:
The action is $ rac{c^4}{16\pi G}\int d^5x\,\sqrt{-g}\,\left(R + \alpha\left(R^2 - 4R_{\mu
u}R^{\mu
u} + R_{\mu
uho\sigma}R^{\mu
uho\sigma}ight)ight)$ with $\ell^2 = 2\alpha$, and the mass $M$ enters through $r_0^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2)$, with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu
u} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha
u}$.

related.text: This black hole with the Gauss-Bonnet term switched off. At $\ell = 0$ the radical is $W = r^2$, the metric function is Tangherlini's $1 - r_0^2/r^2$, and the horizon is back at $r_0$ [boulware1985, garraffo2008].

The second root of the field equations with its mass taken out is anti-de Sitter space of radius $\ell$ in five dimensions. No cosmological constant stands in the action, and the Gauss-Bonnet coupling sets the curvature [boulware1985, garraffo2008].

Black holes of anti-de Sitter space with flat and hyperbolic horizons. Rong-Gen Cai found their counterparts in Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity in 2002, with the same square root in the metric function [cai2002, charmousis2009].

A black hole fed by a stream of radiation, its mass a function of the advanced time $v$. Tsutomu Kobayashi let the mass of this hole depend on $v$ in the same way in 2005, in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, with a null fluid for the radiation [kobayashi2005].

charts.name: Hyperspherical

parameters.description: Mass radius, $r_0^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2)$ with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions, the horizon radius of Tangherlini's black hole of the same mass $M$
Gauss-Bonnet length, $\ell^2 = 2\alpha$ for the coupling $\alpha$ of the Gauss-Bonnet term. For $r_0 > \ell$ the horizon is the sphere $r_h = \sqrt{r_0^2 - \ell^2}$
The radical of the metric function, an area, with $W = r^2$ at $\ell = 0$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\psi$, $\theta$, $\phi$ the angles of the 3-sphere. We write $W = \sqrt{r^4 + 4\ell^2r_0^2}$, in which the metric function is $1 - 2r_0^2/\left(r^2 + W\right)$, Tangherlini's $1 - r_0^2/r^2$ at $\ell = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass radius, $r_0^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2)$ with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions, the horizon radius of Tangherlini's black hole of the same mass $M$
Gauss-Bonnet length, $\ell^2 = 2\alpha$ for the coupling $\alpha$ of the Gauss-Bonnet term. For $r_0 > \ell$ the horizon is the sphere $r_h = \sqrt{r_0^2 - \ell^2}$
The radical of the metric function, an area, with $W = r^2$ at $\ell = 0$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2r_0^2/\left(r^2 + W\right)\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$, and we write $W = \sqrt{r^4 + 4\ell^2r_0^2}$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass radius, $r_0^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2)$ with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions, the horizon radius of Tangherlini's black hole of the same mass $M$
Gauss-Bonnet length, $\ell^2 = 2\alpha$ for the coupling $\alpha$ of the Gauss-Bonnet term. For $r_0 > \ell$ the horizon is the sphere $r_h = \sqrt{r_0^2 - \ell^2}$
The radical of the metric function, an area, with $W = r^2$ at $\ell = 0$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2r_0^2/\left(r^2 + W\right)\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$, and we write $W = \sqrt{r^4 + 4\ell^2r_0^2}$.

charts.name: Hyperspherical, Anti-de Sitter Branch

parameters.description: Mass radius, $r_0^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2)$ with $G$ Newton's constant in five dimensions, the horizon radius of Tangherlini's black hole of the same mass $M$
Gauss-Bonnet length, $\ell^2 = 2\alpha$ for the coupling $\alpha$ of the Gauss-Bonnet term, and the radius of the anti-de Sitter space this branch approaches far away
The radical of the metric function, an area

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ for the other root of the quadratic that fixes the metric function, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We write $W = \sqrt{r^4 + 4\ell^2r_0^2}$, in which the metric function is $1 + 2r_0^2/\left(W - r^2\right)$, the first branch's with $W \to -W$, and it grows as $r^2/\ell^2$ far away. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: C-Metric Accelerating Black Holes
spacetimes.description: An exact vacuum solution describing two black holes that accelerate away from each other, driven by a cosmic string or a strut along their axis of symmetry. With the acceleration set to zero it is the Schwarzschild black hole.

related.text: The C-metric with the acceleration eased off to zero, $\alpha = 0$ [griffiths2006].
The C-metric is one of Robinson and Trautman's solutions, of type D like Schwarzschild's [robinson1962, griffiths2009].
The conical singularity along the axis of the C-metric is a cosmic string under tension, and it pulls the black holes apart [kinnersley1970, griffiths2006].
A black hole with a string through it on both sides, which pull equally, so the hole stays at rest [aryal1986, achucarro1995].
A magnetic field along the axis can do the pulling in place of the string. Frederick Ernst showed in 1976 that it removes the nodal singularity of the charged C-metric [ernst1976].
Tullio Levi-Civita found the static form of the C-metric in 1918, a year before his field of a line of mass [griffiths2009, levicivita1919].
An accelerating spacetime of type D with a regular axis. It needs no string, since the recoil of the light it shines does the pushing [podolsky2008].
A black hole with a spin and a cosmological constant where this one has an acceleration. Plebański and Demiański put all three into one family of solutions [kamran2009, plebanski1976].

A black hole with a spin where this one has an acceleration. Plebański and Demiański's family holds both, and Jerry Griffiths and Jiří Podolský wrote it in 2005 in a form that is Kerr's metric with no acceleration and the C-metric with no rotation [plebanski1976, griffiths2005].

The charged black hole at rest. William Kinnersley and Martin Walker gave the accelerating mass a charge in 1970, and the horizons of their solution resemble Reissner-Nordström's, with one more for the acceleration [kinnersley1970].

The charged black hole of string theory. Fay Dowker, Jerome Gauntlett, David Kastor, and Jennie Traschen wrote the C-metric for a pair of them in 1994, oppositely charged and accelerating apart [dowker1994].

A rotating black hole with a NUT parameter and no acceleration. Jerry Griffiths and Jiří Podolský's form of the Plebański-Demiański family reduces to it when the acceleration is switched off, and to the C-metric when the spin and the twist are [griffiths2005].
Two black holes of opposite charge at rest on one axis. Emparan placed that pair on top of the barrier under which a magnetic field creates the accelerating pair [emparan2000].

charts.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, which is a length; the black hole horizon sits at $r = 2m$
Acceleration, an inverse length, with $2\alpha m < 1$; the acceleration horizon sits at $r = 1/\alpha$
A pure number scaling the angle about the axis; $C = 1/(1 + 2\alpha m)$ makes the half axis $\theta = 0$ regular and leaves a cosmic string along $\theta = \pi$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates of Jerry Griffiths, Pavel Krtouš, and Jiří Podolský, $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Hong-Teo

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, which is a length; the black hole horizon sits at $y = 1/(2\alpha m)$
Acceleration, an inverse length, with $2\alpha m < 1$; the acceleration horizon sits at $y = 1$
A pure number scaling the angle about the axis; $C = 1/(1 + 2\alpha m)$ makes the half axis $x = 1$ regular and leaves a cosmic string along $x = -1$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates of Kenneth Hong and Edward Teo, $(\tau, y, x, \phi)$, all dimensionless and related to the spherical coordinates by $\tau = \alpha ct$, $y = 1/(\alpha r)$, and $x = \cos\theta$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = \dfrac{1}{\alpha^2\left(x + y\right)^2}\left(\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(1 - 2\alpha m y\right)d\tau^2 - \dfrac{dy^2}{\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(1 - 2\alpha m y\right)} + \dfrac{dx^2}{\left(1 - x^2\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m x\right)} + C^2\left(1 - x^2\right)\left(1 + 2\alpha m x\right)d\phi^2\right)

spacetimes.name: Coleman-De Luccia Bubble
spacetimes.description: The spacetime of a false vacuum decaying, found by Sidney Coleman and Frank De Luccia in 1980. A bubble of lower vacuum energy appears by quantum tunnelling, its wall accelerates outward toward the speed of light, and the inside of the bubble is an open universe with no singularity at its start.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: The inside of a bubble whose new vacuum has zero energy. With $a = c\tau$ the open universe inside is Milne's, flat space in hyperbolic slices [bucher1995].
The false vacuum of positive energy outside the wall, written around the bubble's centre with $\rho = \ell\sin(\xi/\ell)$ [coleman1980].
The inside of a bubble whose new vacuum has negative energy. Coleman and De Luccia argued that the smallest disturbance makes it collapse [coleman1980].
The side of the wall where the vacuum energy is zero: the inside of the bubble if our vacuum is what a decay left behind, the outside if ours is the false one [coleman1980].
The inside of every bubble is an open Friedmann universe, $k = -1$, and its $a = 0$ is the light cone of the bubble's centre, a coordinate singularity [coleman1980, bucher1995].
A thin wall with the same flat vacuum on both sides. Its world volume is a hyperboloid as well, de Sitter space of three dimensions [caldwell1996].

charts.name: Outside the Light Cone
domains: \xi = 0 \;\text{(the light cone of the bubble's centre)}

parameters.description: Radius of curvature of the hyperboloid at $\xi$, a length, zero on the light cone $\xi = 0$, where $\partial_\xi\rho = 1$. In a vacuum of cosmological constant $\Lambda$, with $\ell = \sqrt{3/|\Lambda|}$, it is $\xi$ for $\Lambda = 0$, $\ell\sin(\xi/\ell)$ for $\Lambda > 0$, and $\ell\sinh(\xi/\ell)$ for $\Lambda < 0$. Across a thin wall of surface energy density $\sigma$, on the hyperboloid of radius $\bar\rho$, $\rho$ is continuous and $\partial_\xi\rho$ drops by $4\pi G\sigma\bar\rho/c^4$

charts.convention: We use Coleman and De Luccia's coordinates outside the light cone of the event the bubble is centred on: $\xi$ is the proper distance along the curves of constant $\psi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$, zero on that light cone, and $\psi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ are coordinates on the hyperboloid of events at one $\xi$. The rapidity $\psi$ is a pure number, itself the chart's $x^0$, and we leave the function $\rho(\xi)$ free. In the geodesic equations a dot is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Open Universe
domains: \tau = 0 \;\text{(the light cone of the bubble's centre)}

parameters.description: Scale factor of the open universe inside the bubble, a length, zero on the light cone $\tau = 0$, where $a' = 1$. In a vacuum of cosmological constant $\Lambda$, with $\ell = \sqrt{3/|\Lambda|}$, it is $c\tau$ for $\Lambda = 0$, $\ell\sinh(c\tau/\ell)$ for $\Lambda > 0$, and $\ell\sin(c\tau/\ell)$ for $\Lambda < 0$, which returns to zero at $c\tau = \pi\ell$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, \chi, \theta, \phi)$ inside the future light cone of the event the bubble is centred on, with $\tau$ the proper time since that light cone along the comoving world lines and $\chi$ a rapidity, a pure number. We leave the scale factor $a(\tau)$ free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, a prime is the derivative along that chart time, $a' = da/d(c\tau)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Open Universe, Conformal Time
domains: \eta \to -\infty \;\text{(the light cone of the bubble's centre)}

parameters.description: Scale factor of the open universe inside the bubble, a length. In a vacuum of cosmological constant $\Lambda$, with $\ell = \sqrt{3/|\Lambda|}$, it is $\ell e^{\eta}$ for $\Lambda = 0$, $-\ell/\sinh\eta$ on $\eta < 0$ for $\Lambda > 0$, and $\ell/\cosh\eta$ for $\Lambda < 0$

charts.convention: We use the conformal time $\eta$ of the open universe inside the bubble, a pure number with $a\,d\eta = c\,d\tau$ for the proper time $\tau$ of the comoving world lines, and the comoving $\chi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$. The conformal time is itself the chart's $x^0$, and we leave the scale factor $a(\eta)$ free. A prime is $d/d\eta$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Static, Inside the Wall

parameters.description: Cosmological constant of the true vacuum, inside the wall, of either sign, carrying an inverse length squared

Areal radius of the wall, a length, with $r_w^2 = \bar\rho^2 + \left(1 - \Lambda_T\bar\rho^2/3\right)\tanh^2\left(\sqrt{\Lambda_T/3}\,ct\right)/(\Lambda_T/3)$ for a wall born at rest with the radius $\bar\rho$ at $t = 0$; that is $\bar\rho^2 + c^2t^2$ at $\Lambda_T = 0$, and the hyperbolic tangent is a tangent for $\Lambda_T < 0$

charts.convention: We use the static coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of the true vacuum about the bubble's centre, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Static, Outside the Wall

parameters.description: Cosmological constant of the false vacuum, outside the wall, of either sign, carrying an inverse length squared

Areal radius of the wall, a length, with $r_w^2 = \bar\rho^2 + \left(1 - \Lambda_F\bar\rho^2/3\right)\tanh^2\left(\sqrt{\Lambda_F/3}\,ct\right)/(\Lambda_F/3)$ for a wall born at rest with the radius $\bar\rho$ at $t = 0$; that is $\bar\rho^2 + c^2t^2$ at $\Lambda_F = 0$, and the hyperbolic tangent is a tangent for $\Lambda_F < 0$

charts.convention: We use the static coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of the false vacuum about the bubble's centre, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Curzon-Chazy Particle
spacetimes.description: A static, axially symmetric vacuum field whose Weyl potential is Newton's potential of a point mass, found by Jean Chazy in 1924 and H. E. J. Curzon in 1925. Its singularity is a naked ring of infinite circumference, and the curvature there depends on the direction of approach.
spacetimes.convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ is a length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: Both are Weyl fields built on a Newtonian potential, that of a rod of length $r_s$ for Schwarzschild and that of a point for Curzon and Chazy [weyl1917, bicak2000].
The Weyl field of a rod. In the limit of the rod shrunk to a point at fixed mass it becomes the Curzon-Chazy particle [herrera1999].

Two Kerr black holes at rest on one axis. The axis between them is singular, as the line joining two Curzon-Chazy particles is, and no choice of spins removes the singularity [kramer1980, neugebauer2009].

A cloud of rotating dust built on the potential of a point, as the Curzon-Chazy particle is. Its singularity at the origin is directional too: the curvature diverges along the axis and dies away in the equatorial plane [bonnor1977cloud, astesiano2024].

Static discs of counterrotating dust, Weyl fields built on the Newtonian potential of a disc. In the limit of the disc shrunk to a point at fixed mass the field is the Curzon-Chazy particle's, which itself arises as the metric of a counterrotating disc [bicak1993].
Bonnor's pair of extremal black holes. In Weyl's coordinates each of the two is a single point of the axis, as the Curzon-Chazy particle is [emparanteo2001].

charts.name: Weyl

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass at spatial infinity
Distance from the origin in the flat space of Weyl's coordinates; Weyl's two functions are $\psi = -m/R$ and $\gamma = -m^2\rho^2/(2R^4)$

charts.convention: We use Weyl's canonical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, and write $R = \sqrt{\rho^2 + z^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass at spatial infinity

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ with $\rho = r\sin\theta$ and $z = r\cos\theta$, so that $r$ is Weyl's $R$, and with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Damour-Solodukhin Wormhole
spacetimes.description: Schwarzschild's metric with a small constant $\lambda^2$ added to $-g_{tt}$, which Thibault Damour and Sergey Solodukhin wrote down in 2007. The horizon becomes the throat of a static wormhole joining two asymptotically flat regions, and for small $\lambda$ an observer needs a time of order $(r_s/c)\ln(1/\lambda^2)$ to tell it from a black hole.
spacetimes.convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: At $\lambda = 0$ the throat is Schwarzschild's horizon and the wormhole is his black hole. For any other $\lambda$ a moment of time is the same Flamm's paraboloid, with a throat that stays open [damour2007].
At $\lambda = 0$ the wormhole written in Einstein and Rosen's $u$ is their neutral bridge of 1935, whose throat is a horizon [einstein1935].

The general static wormhole a traveller could cross, with any redshift function $\Phi$ and shape function $b$. Damour and Solodukhin's is the one with $b = r_s$ and $e^{2\Phi} = 1 - r_s/r + \lambda^2$ [morris1988, nandi2022].

Visser's wormhole cut from Schwarzschild's exterior, the other wormhole made to pass for a black hole. Cardoso, Franzin, and Pani dropped a particle through one with its throat just outside $r_s$ and heard a black hole's ringdown, with the wormhole's own modes arriving late [cardoso2016prl].

Another member of Morris and Thorne's family, with $\Phi = 0$ and $b = \ell^2/r$. Its clocks run at one rate everywhere, where Damour and Solodukhin's slow by the factor $\lambda$ at the throat [ellis1973, bronnikov1973, damour2007].

Simpson and Visser's one parameter change of Schwarzschild's metric, made in the radius, $r \to \sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$. Its wormhole has a throat of radius $a > r_s$, and for smaller $a$ it is a black hole with no singularity [simpson2019].

The black hole of three dimensions, where the change was first made. Solodukhin added $\lambda^2$ to its $g_{tt}$ in 2005, which removes the horizon and leaves a wormhole whose perturbations evolve quasiperiodically [solodukhin2005].

charts.name: Damour-Solodukhin

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the areal radius of the throat
Dimensionless constant, $\lambda > 0$; at $\lambda = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ on either side of the throat, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{r_s^2\left(4\left(r - r_s\right)\left(\left(1 + \lambda^2\right)r - r_s\right) - \lambda^2\,r\,r_s\right)^2}{4r^6\left(\left(1 + \lambda^2\right)r - r_s\right)^4} + \dfrac{2r_s^2\left(r - r_s\right)^2}{r^6\left(\left(1 + \lambda^2\right)r - r_s\right)^2} + \dfrac{6r_s^2}{r^6}

charts.name: Rescaled Time

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the areal radius of the throat
Dimensionless constant, $\lambda > 0$; at $\lambda = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ on either side of the throat, with $r$ the areal radius and $t$ the proper time of a clock at rest far away, $\sqrt{1 + \lambda^2}$ times the time of Damour and Solodukhin's chart. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{r_s^2\left(4\left(r - r_s\right)\left(\left(1 + \lambda^2\right)r - r_s\right) - \lambda^2\,r\,r_s\right)^2}{4r^6\left(\left(1 + \lambda^2\right)r - r_s\right)^4} + \dfrac{2r_s^2\left(r - r_s\right)^2}{r^6\left(\left(1 + \lambda^2\right)r - r_s\right)^2} + \dfrac{6r_s^2}{r^6}

charts.name: Through the Throat

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the areal radius of the throat
Dimensionless constant, $\lambda > 0$; at $\lambda = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ the proper time of a clock at rest far away and $\rho$ dimensionless, changing sign at the throat. The areal radius is $r = r_s\left(2 + \lambda^2(1 + \cosh\rho)\right)/2(1 + \lambda^2)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.

charts.name: Isotropic
domains: r \to 0 \;\text{(the far end of the other side)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the areal radius of the throat
Dimensionless constant, $\lambda > 0$; at $\lambda = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the isotropic radius, so the areal radius is $r\left(1 + r_s/4r\right)^2$ and $r \to r_s^2/16r$ exchanges the two sides of the throat. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{16777216r^6\,r_s^2}{\left(4r + r_s\right)^{12}}\left(\dfrac{4\left(\left(4r - r_s\right)^2\left(\left(4r - r_s\right)^2 + \lambda^2\left(4r + r_s\right)^2\right) - 4\lambda^2\,r\,r_s\left(4r + r_s\right)^2\right)^2}{\left(\left(4r - r_s\right)^2 + \lambda^2\left(4r + r_s\right)^2\right)^4} + \dfrac{2\left(4r - r_s\right)^4}{\left(\left(4r - r_s\right)^2 + \lambda^2\left(4r + r_s\right)^2\right)^2} + 6\right)

charts.name: Einstein-Rosen

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the areal radius of the throat
Dimensionless constant, $\lambda > 0$; at $\lambda = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, u, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $u^2 = r - r_s$, so $u$ is the square root of a length and changes sign at the throat. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.

spacetimes.name: de Sitter
spacetimes.description: The maximally symmetric vacuum solution with constant positive curvature, driven by a positive cosmological constant. It models an exponentially expanding empty universe and describes both inflation and the far future of our cosmos.

related.text: A black hole placed in de Sitter space, so that a static observer sits between two horizons. At $r_s = 0$ it is de Sitter space.

The homogeneous, isotropic universe with any matter in it. Georges Lemaître and Howard Robertson showed that de Sitter space is one, with flat space and a scale factor growing exponentially [lemaitre1925, robertson1928].
The same geometry with its curvature reversed in sign, the vacuum of a negative cosmological constant. Its infinity is timelike [hawking1973].
De Sitter space with its expansion switched off, $\Lambda \to 0$, where the cosmological horizon recedes to infinity.
Einstein's universe of the same year, dust in balance against $\Lambda$ [einstein1917]. De Sitter space maps conformally onto a strip of it, where its conformal diagram is drawn [hawking1973].
Another vacuum with a positive cosmological constant, the product of de Sitter space of two dimensions and a sphere of the same radius [ortaggio2002].

A black hole with de Sitter space at its centre. Inside its inner horizon Bardeen's metric approaches de Sitter's static patch, which keeps the centre regular, and in the limit $g \to \infty$ at fixed $r_s/g^3$ it is de Sitter's everywhere [ansoldi2008].

A black hole whose core is a ball of de Sitter space with $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$ whatever the mass. In the limit $m \to \infty$ at fixed $\ell$ the whole metric is de Sitter's [hayward2006, frolov2016].
De Sitter space with a rotating black hole put in. With the mass taken out again, Carter's metric is de Sitter space in spheroidal coordinates [akcay2011].
De Sitter space with charged black holes in it, each with a charge equal to its mass, carried along by the expansion or the contraction [kastor1993].

Schwarzschild's star of uniform density. Pawel Mazur and Emil Mottola showed in 2015 that with its radius taken down to its Schwarzschild radius the inside is a static patch of de Sitter space, with pressure $-\rho c^2$ throughout [mazur2015].

The homogeneous universes that expand at different rates in different directions. With a positive cosmological constant the differences die away: Robert Wald proved in 1983 that every expanding Bianchi universe but some of type IX approaches de Sitter space exponentially [wald1983].

A domain wall is a de Sitter space of one dimension fewer. In the flat space on either side the wall is the hyperboloid $X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1/k^2 + c^2T^2$, and the metric induced on it is de Sitter's in $2 + 1$ dimensions [ipser1984, caldwell1996].
De Sitter space with a bubble of lower vacuum energy growing in it, the way a false vacuum decays [coleman1980].

A universe of radiation that also contracts, bounces, and expands with no singularity, and keeps the strong energy condition that de Sitter's violates. It has no closed trapped surface, and its slices of constant time are open [senovilla1998, chinea1992].
A ball of de Sitter space inside a thin shell, with Schwarzschild's vacuum outside. The vacuum within pushes outward on the shell, and no horizon forms [mazur2004].

De Sitter's static metric with a black hole added and $\Lambda r^2/3$ replaced by a power of the radius, $(r_q/r)^{3w+1}$. At $w = -1$ and $r_s = 0$ it is de Sitter's, with $\Lambda = 3/r_q^2$ [kiselev2003].

charts.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, $\Lambda > 0$, carrying an inverse length squared. The horizon sits at $r = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$ and the expansion rate of the flat slicing is $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}\right)c^2 dt^2 + \dfrac{dr^2}{1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}} + r^2 d\Omega^2

charts.name: Flat Slicing

parameters.description: Hubble rate, $H = c\sqrt{\Lambda/3}$, so that $\dfrac{3H^2}{c^2} = \Lambda$ and the horizon radius of the static patch is $c/H$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving lengths, and the Hubble rate $H$ in place of $\Lambda$, related by $3H^2/c^2 = \Lambda$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Gibbons-Maeda-Garfinkle-Horowitz-Strominger Dilaton Black Hole
spacetimes.description: The static, spherically symmetric charged black hole of low energy string theory, a solution of Einstein's equations with a Maxwell field and a scalar field, the dilaton, coupled to it. On the plane of time and radius its metric is Schwarzschild's, with one horizon at the Schwarzschild radius for every charge and no inner horizon, and the area of its spheres vanishes at the singularity.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and $r_s$ and $r_d$ are lengths. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: The black hole with no charge, $r_d = 0$. With charge, the plane of $t$ and $r$ keeps Schwarzschild's metric and the spheres shrink [horowitz1992].
The charged black hole of Einstein-Maxwell theory, with no dilaton. It has an inner horizon, and the dilaton black hole has none [horowitz1992].

The extreme magnetic black hole of the same family with the dilaton coupled at strength $\sqrt{3}$, Kaluza and Klein's value. Lifted to five dimensions its singularity goes away and it is a smooth vacuum solution [duff1994].
The charged, rotating black hole of Einstein-Maxwell theory. Ashoke Sen built its counterpart in heterotic string theory in 1992, a black hole with mass, charge, and angular momentum [sen1992].

Two black holes accelerating apart. Dowker, Gauntlett, Kastor, and Traschen generalised it in 1994 to a pair of oppositely charged dilaton black holes, and used it to describe their creation in a magnetic field [dowker1994].
In the limit of the extremal magnetic charge, the region around the horizon is closely approximated by Witten's black hole in two dimensions times a sphere [giddings1992].

The charged holes of Kaluza and Klein's theory, where the scalar field couples with strength $\sqrt{3}$ and records the length of a fifth dimension. Their extremal limit has a horizon of zero area too, unless both charges are present [horowitz2012].

charts.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components of the Einstein metric in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the Einstein metric, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the Einstein metric, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$.

charts.name: String Metric, Magnetic Charge

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, and take components of the string metric $e^{2\varphi}g_{\mu\nu}$ of the magnetically charged hole, with $g_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein metric and $e^{-2\varphi} = 1 - r_d/r$, in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: String Metric, Electric Charge

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components of the string metric $e^{2\varphi}g_{\mu\nu}$ of the electrically charged hole, with $g_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein metric and $e^{2\varphi} = 1 - r_d/r$, in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Double Kerr Solution
spacetimes.description: Two Kerr black holes on one axis of symmetry, the stationary vacuum solution Dietrich Kramer and Gernot Neugebauer built in 1980 by two Bäcklund transformations of flat space. The repulsion between the spins does not balance the attraction of the masses, so a strut on the axis between the horizons holds the holes apart.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: One of the two holes on its own. A single Bäcklund transformation of flat space returns the Kerr-NUT solution, which holds Kerr's black hole, and two return the pair [neugebauer2012].

One hole on its own with the spin switched off. With both spins switched off the pair is Rudolf Bach and Hermann Weyl's two Schwarzschild bodies of 1922, with a singular stretch of axis between them [bach1922, neugebauer2012].

Black holes that do stand still side by side. Each carries a charge equal to its mass, and the electric repulsion balances the attraction, which the repulsion between two spins does not [hartle1972, neugebauer2009].
Spinning sources that do stay in balance. Each carries a charge equal to its mass, and the electric repulsion holds the spinning sources in a stationary configuration [perjes1971, israel1972].

Jean Chazy and H. E. J. Curzon each presented two point particles at rest on one axis, and the line joining the particles is singular as the axis between the two holes is [chazy1924, curzon1925, einstein1936twobody].

Two black holes at rest with no strut between them, for one moment only: the slice of space from which Susan Hahn and Richard Lindquist first computed two holes colliding head on [brill1963, hahn1964, holst2016].

charts.name: Weyl-Lewis-Papapetrou
domains: \rho = 0,\; a_1 \le z \le a_2 \;\text{and}\; a_3 \le z \le a_4 \;\text{(the two horizons)}

parameters.description: Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$, with $-f$ the norm of the Killing vector $\partial_t$ in the chart $x^0 = ct$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $f\left(\partial_\rho^2f + \dfrac{1}{\rho}\partial_\rho f + \partial_z^2f\right) = \left(\partial_\rho f\right)^2 + \left(\partial_zf\right)^2 - \dfrac{f^4}{\rho^2}\left(\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right)$ together with the equations for $\omega$ and $\gamma$; for two Kerr black holes $f$ is the real part of the Ernst potential $\mathcal{E} = D_-/D_+$, with $D_\pm = X^\pm_{12}X^\pm_{34} - X^\pm_{14}X^\pm_{32}$, $X^\pm_{ik} = \dfrac{\alpha_ir_i + \alpha_kr_k}{a_i - a_k} \pm 1$, and $r_j = \sqrt{\rho^2 + (z - a_j)^2}$, where $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, and $a_4$ are the ends of the two horizons on the axis, lengths in increasing order, and each $\alpha_j$ is a complex number of modulus one

Function of $\rho$ and $z$, a length, with $f\omega$ the product of the Killing vectors $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\phi$; in a vacuum $\partial_\rho\left(\dfrac{f^2}{\rho}\partial_\rho\omega\right) + \partial_z\left(\dfrac{f^2}{\rho}\partial_z\omega\right) = 0$, and for two Kerr black holes $\partial_\rho\omega = -\dfrac{\rho}{f^2}\partial_z\chi$ and $\partial_z\omega = \dfrac{\rho}{f^2}\partial_\rho\chi$, where $\chi$ is the imaginary part of $\mathcal{E}$

Dimensionless function of $\rho$ and $z$ fixed by $f$ and $\omega$ through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \dfrac{\rho}{4f^2}\left(\left(\partial_\rho f\right)^2 - \left(\partial_zf\right)^2\right) - \dfrac{f^2}{4\rho}\left(\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 - \left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right)$ and $\partial_z\gamma = \dfrac{\rho}{2f^2}\partial_\rho f\,\partial_zf - \dfrac{f^2}{2\rho}\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_z\omega$, and zero on a regular axis; for two Kerr black holes $e^{2\gamma} = \dfrac{\mathrm{Re}\left(D_-D_+^*\right)}{C\,r_1r_2r_3r_4}$, where the star is complex conjugation and the constant $C$ makes $\gamma$ vanish far from the holes; inside an ergoregion, where $f < 0$, $e^{2\gamma}$ is negative with $f$, so $\gamma$ has the imaginary part $\pi/2$ there
