charts.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Joshua Baines, Thomas Berry, Alex Simpson, and Matt Visser, whose $t$ carries dimensions of time and is the proper time of an observer falling from rest far away with no angular momentum. Every component is exact for the line element as written, which agrees with Hartle and Thorne's to first order in $a$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Hayward Regular Black Hole
spacetimes.description: A black hole with two horizons and a regular centre, Schwarzschild's metric far away and de Sitter space at the core. Sean Hayward wrote it down in 2006 and let its mass change in time, so that a region of trapped surfaces forms, evaporates, and leaves neither a singularity nor an event horizon.
spacetimes.convention: The mass is the length $m = GM/c^2$, and the length $\ell$ sets the cosmological constant $3/\ell^2$ of the de Sitter core at the centre. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.

related.text: Hayward's black hole at $\ell = 0$, where the core shrinks away and the singularity is back, with $r_s = 2m$ [hayward2006].
The same two horizons and the same tower of regions. Reissner-Nordström's has a timelike singularity at $r = 0$, and Hayward's a regular centre [hayward2006].
The first regular black hole, from 1968, with $(r^2 + g^2)^{3/2}$ where Hayward's has $r^3 + 2m\ell^2$. Hayward called his own "similar to the Bardeen black hole" [hayward2006].

The core. Near the centre $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$, de Sitter's static metric with $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$, and as $m \to \infty$ at fixed $\ell$ the whole metric becomes de Sitter's [hayward2006, frolov2016].
The forming and evaporating hole at $\ell = 0$, and at large radius for every $\ell$. Vaidya's ingoing radiation makes a singularity at the centre [hayward2006].

Another black hole with no singularity. Simpson and Visser set theirs apart from the regular black holes of Bardeen and Hayward: it opens through a throat of radius $a$ where Hayward's closes over a regular centre [simpson2019].
A ball of de Sitter space under a thin shell with Schwarzschild's vacuum outside, a collapsed star with a de Sitter core and no horizon [mazur2004].

Ori's model of a charged hole with radiation crossing it, whose mass function grows without limit at the inner horizon. Carried over to Hayward's metric it gives an exponentially growing mass at the inner horizon as well [carballorubio2021].

The evaporating hole Hayward took the surface of pair creation from, with negative energy falling in and positive energy going out. Hiscock's keeps its singularity, and the last point of it is naked [hayward2006, hiscock1981].

charts.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Mass as a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Length of the de Sitter core, with $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$ near the centre; $\kappa_\pm$ are the surface gravities of the horizons $r_\pm$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$. For $\ell < 4m/3\sqrt{3}$ the horizons $r_- < r_+$ are the two positive roots of $r^3 - 2mr^2 + 2m\ell^2$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass as a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Length of the de Sitter core, with $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$ near the centre; $\kappa_\pm$ are the surface gravities of the horizons $r_\pm$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2mr^2/(r^3 + 2m\ell^2)\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$. For $\ell < 4m/3\sqrt{3}$ the horizons $r_- < r_+$ are the two positive roots of $r^3 - 2mr^2 + 2m\ell^2$.

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass as a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Length of the de Sitter core, with $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$ near the centre; $\kappa_\pm$ are the surface gravities of the horizons $r_\pm$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2mr^2/(r^3 + 2m\ell^2)\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$. For $\ell < 4m/3\sqrt{3}$ the horizons $r_- < r_+$ are the two positive roots of $r^3 - 2mr^2 + 2m\ell^2$.

charts.name: Forming and Evaporating

parameters.description: Mass function of advanced time, a length, $m = GM/c^2$; $m_0$ is its greatest value in the drawings
Length of the de Sitter core, with $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$ near the centre; $\kappa_\pm$ are the surface gravities of the horizons $r_\pm$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ a length and the mass a function $m(v)$ of it. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

spacetimes.name: Hiscock's Evaporating Black Hole
spacetimes.description: A black hole that forms and then radiates itself away, built by William Hiscock in 1981 from Vaidya's metric. Inside a surface just outside the apparent horizon negative energy falls in and lowers the mass, and outside it positive energy carries the same mass off to infinity. The event horizon ends after a finite time, and the last point of the singularity is naked.
spacetimes.convention: The mass is the length $m = GM/c^2$ and the null times are lengths, so no factor of $c$ or $G$ stands in a component. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: Both halves of the model. Vaidya's ingoing metric with a falling mass shrinks the hole, and his outgoing metric carries the radiation away [hiscock1981outgoing].
The hole between its birth and the start of the evaporation, and the field far away until the first of the radiation passes [lubbe2009].
The space inside the collapsing shell, and the space left once the last of the radiation has gone by [martindussaud2019].

The same pair of streams, negative energy in and positive energy out, around a black hole with a regular centre. Hayward built it by "adapting an idea of Hiscock", and it leaves neither a singularity nor an event horizon [hayward2006].

charts.name: Ingoing Vaidya
domains: r = R \;\text{(the surface of pair creation)}

parameters.description: Mass function of advanced time, a length, $m = GM/c^2$: zero before the hole forms, falling while negative energy flows in, and zero once the hole is gone; $m_0$ is its greatest value in the drawings
Areal radius of the surface where the pairs are created, a length, with $R > 2m$ while the hole evaporates; the outgoing radiation lies beyond it

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ constant along ingoing light rays and $r$ the areal radius. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Outgoing Vaidya
domains: r = R \;\text{(the surface of pair creation)}

parameters.description: Mass function of retarded time, a length, $m = GM/c^2$, the mass measured by a distant observer at the retarded time $u$; on the surface of pair creation it equals the mass inside; $m_0$ is its greatest value in the drawings
Areal radius of the surface where the pairs are created, a length, with $R > 2m$ while the hole evaporates; the ingoing negative energy lies inside it

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u$ constant along outgoing light rays and $r$ the areal radius. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Flat Double Null
charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, v, \theta, \phi)$, the retarded and advanced times of flat space, with the areal radius $r = (v - u)/2$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

spacetimes.name: Israel's Collapsing Shell of Dust
spacetimes.description: A thin spherical shell of dust falling under its own weight, with flat spacetime inside it and Schwarzschild's vacuum outside. Werner Israel solved its motion in 1966 with the junction conditions he wrote for a surface that carries matter. The event horizon forms at the centre of the flat interior before the shell arrives.
spacetimes.convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: The outside of the shell. The mass in it is the energy of the shell, the dust's energy of motion less the binding energy [poisson2004].
The inside of the shell, flat until the shell arrives. The event horizon starts at its centre and crosses it at the speed of light.
The collapse of a whole ball of dust, with a piece of a closed universe inside where the shell has flat space [oppenheimersnyder1939].
The shell of light, the limit $m \to 0$ of the shell of dust at fixed $M$, which falls along one ingoing ray [adler2005].
Two Schwarzschild exteriors joined at a throat by the same junction conditions, on a shell of negative energy density [visser1989nuclphysb].
A shell that stays put, with de Sitter space inside it where the falling shell has flat space [visser2004].

charts.name: Flat Interior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu = r_s/2$ falls from rest at infinity, and a heavier one from rest at a finite radius
Areal radius of the shell, a length. With $\tau$ the proper time of the dust and $\gamma = r_s/2\mu + \mu/2R$, it falls as $dR/d(c\tau) = -\sqrt{\gamma^2 - 1}$ while $dT/d\tau = \gamma$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(T, r, \theta, \phi)$ inside the shell, with $T$ the time of an observer at rest at the centre, carrying dimensions of time, and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Schwarzschild Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu = r_s/2$ falls from rest at infinity, and a heavier one from rest at a finite radius

Areal radius of the shell, a length. With $\tau$ the proper time of the dust and $\beta = r_s/2\mu - \mu/2R$, it falls as $dR/d(c\tau) = -\sqrt{\beta^2 - 1 + r_s/R}$ while $(1 - r_s/R)\,dt/d\tau = \beta$, and it reaches $r_s$ only as $t \to \infty$

charts.convention: We use Schwarzschild coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ outside the shell, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, the same $r$ as inside. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass $M$ measured outside the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Rest mass $m$ of the dust as a length, $\mu = Gm/c^2$; a shell with $\mu = r_s/2$ falls from rest at infinity, and a heavier one from rest at a finite radius

Areal radius of the shell, a length. With $\tau$ the proper time of the dust and $\beta = r_s/2\mu - \mu/2R$, it falls as $dR/d(c\tau) = -\sqrt{\beta^2 - 1 + r_s/R}$ while $dv/d(c\tau) = 1/\left(\beta + \sqrt{\beta^2 - 1 + r_s/R}\right)$, through $r_s$ to $R = 0$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$ outside the shell, with the advanced time $v = ct + r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ a length, constant along ingoing light rays, and $r$ the areal radius. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

spacetimes.name: Israel-Wilson-Perjés Spinning Charged Sources
spacetimes.description: Majumdar and Papapetrou's balanced charges set spinning: the stationary electrovacuum fields built from a complex solution of Laplace's equation, found by Zoltán Perjés in 1971 and by Werner Israel and Gordon Wilson in 1972. Every source carries a charge equal to its mass, and the family holds Kerr and Newman's spinning body with that charge, a naked singularity, and a charged NUT space.
spacetimes.convention:
We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu
u} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha
u}$. The complex potential $U$ solves Laplace's equation on flat space, and $
abla 	imes \vec{\omega} = i\left(U
abla ar{U} -  ar{U}
abla Uight)$.

related.text: The same balanced charges at rest. A real $U$ has $\vec{\omega} = 0$, and the metric is Majumdar and Papapetrou's [hartle1972].

One source at an imaginary place is Kerr and Newman's metric with charge equal to mass, in the radius $r + m$ [hartle1972]. With that much charge any spin leaves the ring singularity naked [kallosh1994iwp].

One source of complex mass is NUT space with a charge added, Brill's solution with charge radius $\sqrt{m^2 + l^2}$ [hartle1972, brill1964]. It keeps the singular axis of NUT space, which Misner's periodic time removes [misner1963].

Tod's other class. A spacetime with a supercovariantly constant spinor is one of Israel, Wilson, and Perjés's fields where the spinor's Killing vector is timelike, and a pp-wave where it is null everywhere [tod1983, chrusciel2006].
Two spinning black holes with no charge, on one axis. Their spins do not balance their attraction, and a strut on the axis holds them apart [kramer1980, neugebauer2009].

charts.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: Dimensionless modulus of the potential, $W = |U|$; no component assumes $U$ harmonic
The component $\omega_\phi$ of $\vec{\omega}$, a length, fixed by $U$ up to a constant; no component assumes its equation

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$ for axisymmetric fields, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. The metric holds $W = |U|$ and the one component $\omega = \omega_\phi$, with $\partial_z\omega = -2\rho\,\mathrm{Im}\left(\bar{U}\,\partial_\rho U\right)$ and $\partial_\rho\omega = 2\rho\,\mathrm{Im}\left(\bar{U}\,\partial_z U\right)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{16W^6\,\rho^2\left(2\rho^2\,\partial_\rho^2 W\,\partial_z^2 W + 2\rho\,\partial_\rho W\,\partial_\rho^2 W + 2\rho\,\partial_\rho W\,\partial_z^2 W + 4\rho^2\left(\partial_\rho\partial_z W\right)^2 + 3\rho^2\left(\partial_\rho^2 W\right)^2 + 3\rho^2\left(\partial_z^2 W\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_\rho W\right)^2\right) - 32W^5\,\rho^3\left(12\rho\,\partial_\rho W\,\partial_\rho\partial_z W\,\partial_z W - \rho\,\partial_\rho^2 W\left(\partial_z W\right)^2 + 5\rho\left(\partial_\rho W\right)^2\,\partial_\rho^2 W - \rho\left(\partial_\rho W\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 W + 5\rho\left(\partial_z W\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 W - \partial_\rho W\left(\partial_z W\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\rho W\right)^3\right) + 8W^4\left(56\rho^4\left(\partial_\rho W\right)^2\left(\partial_z W\right)^2 + 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_\rho^2\omega + 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\partial_z\omega\,\partial_z\omega - 2\rho^2\left(\partial_\rho\partial_z\omega\right)^2 - \rho^2\left(\partial_\rho^2\omega\right)^2 - \rho^2\left(\partial_z^2\omega\right)^2 + 28\rho^4\left(\partial_\rho W\right)^4 + 28\rho^4\left(\partial_z W\right)^4 - \left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 - 2\left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right) + 16W^3\,\rho\left(5\rho\,\partial_\rho W\,\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_\rho^2\omega - \rho\,\partial_\rho W\,\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_z^2\omega + 6\rho\,\partial_\rho W\,\partial_\rho\partial_z\omega\,\partial_z\omega - 4\rho\,\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_\rho\partial_z W\,\partial_z\omega + 6\rho\,\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_\rho\partial_z\omega\,\partial_z W - \rho\,\partial_\rho^2\omega\,\partial_z W\,\partial_z\omega + 5\rho\,\partial_z W\,\partial_z\omega\,\partial_z^2\omega + \partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_z W\,\partial_z\omega - 2\rho\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2\,\partial_\rho^2 W - 2\rho\left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 W - 7\partial_\rho W\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 - 8\partial_\rho W\left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right) + 8W^2\,\rho^2\left(16\partial_\rho W\,\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_z W\,\partial_z\omega - 21\left(\partial_\rho W\right)^2\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 - 29\left(\partial_\rho W\right)^2\left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2 - 29\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2\left(\partial_z W\right)^2 - 21\left(\partial_z W\right)^2\left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right) + 11\left(\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z\omega\right)^2\right)^2}{4W^{12}\rho^4}

charts.name: Oblate Spheroidal

parameters.description: Mass parameter of the source, $m = GM/c^2$, equal to its charge radius
Spin per unit mass, $a = J/(Mc)$, a length; $a = 0$ is one hole of Majumdar and Papapetrou's
Vanishes on the ring $r = 0$, $\theta = \pi/2$, where $U$ is infinite and $\partial_t$ is null
Vanishes on the ring singularity, $r = -m$ on the equator

charts.convention: We use oblate spheroidal coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of flat space, $\rho = \sqrt{r^2 + a^2}\sin\theta$ and $z = r\cos\theta$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and write $\Sigma_0$ and $\Sigma$ as the parameters define them. The one source is $U = 1 + m/(r + ia\cos\theta)$, and Boyer and Lindquist's radius is $r + m$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{48m^2\left(\left(r + m\right)^6 - 15a^2\left(r + m\right)^4\cos^2\theta + 15a^4\left(r + m\right)^2\cos^4\theta - a^6\cos^6\theta\right) - 96m^3\left(r + m\right)\left(\left(r + m\right)^4 - 10a^2\left(r + m\right)^2\cos^2\theta + 5a^4\cos^4\theta\right) + 8m^4\left(7\left(r + m\right)^4 - 34a^2\left(r + m\right)^2\cos^2\theta + 7a^4\cos^4\theta\right)}{\Sigma^6}

charts.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Mass parameter, $m = GM/c^2$, a length; the horizon is $r = m$
NUT parameter, a length; the electric and magnetic charge radii are $m$ and $l$, and $l = 0$ is one hole of Majumdar and Papapetrou's

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ for the one source of complex mass, $U = 1 + (m + il)/(r - m)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r - m$ the radius of flat space. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{\left(r - m\right)^2}{r^2 + l^2}\left(c\,dt + 2l\cos\theta\,d\phi\right)^2 + \dfrac{r^2 + l^2}{\left(r - m\right)^2}dr^2 + \left(r^2 + l^2\right)\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right)

spacetimes.name: Kaluza-Klein Black Holes
spacetimes.description: The charged black holes of gravity in five dimensions with the fifth dimension a small circle, vacuum solutions that four dimensions see as black holes with an electric charge, a magnetic charge, or both, and a scalar field. The electric hole is Schwarzschild's black string set moving around the circle, and Gary Gibbons and David Wiltshire classified the family in 1986.
spacetimes.convention: The lengths $r_s$, $q$, and $p$ fix the mass and the charges. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.

related.text: The hole with no charge, $q = r_s$ and $p = r_s$: Schwarzschild's black hole at every point of the circle. Set it moving around the circle and it is the electric hole [horowitz2012].
The magnetic hole with its horizon taken away, $r_s = 0$, where $p = 4m$. The circle then closes smoothly at $r = 0$ and no singularity is left [horowitz2012].
With equal electric and magnetic charges the scalar field is constant, and the metric orthogonal to the circles is Reissner and Nordström's, with both of its horizons [larsen2000].

The charged black hole of string theory, whose scalar field couples to the Maxwell field with strength $1$ where Kaluza and Klein's couples with strength $\sqrt{3}$. Gibbons and Maeda found the charged holes for every coupling [gibbons1988, rasheed1995].

The electric hole at the speed of light, $r_s = 0$ with $q$ held fixed, is a plane fronted wave in five dimensions with the profile $q/r$, the counterpart there of Aichelburg and Sexl's shock [horowitz2012].

charts.name: Electric Charge

parameters.description: Radius of the horizon, the Schwarzschild radius of the black string before the boost

Charge length, $q = r_s\cosh^2\alpha$ for a boost of rapidity $\alpha$ along the circle; $q \ge r_s$, and $q = r_s$ is no charge. In units with $G = c = 1$ in four dimensions the mass is $M = (q + r_s)/4$ and the electric charge $Q = \sqrt{q(q - r_s)}/2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi, y)$, Schwarzschild's with the length $y$ around the fifth dimension added, and $t$ carrying dimensions of time. The circle of $y$ has any length $L$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Radius of the horizon, the Schwarzschild radius of the black string before the boost

Charge length, $q = r_s\cosh^2\alpha$ for a boost of rapidity $\alpha$ along the circle; $q \ge r_s$, and $q = r_s$ is no charge. In units with $G = c = 1$ in four dimensions the mass is $M = (q + r_s)/4$ and the electric charge $Q = \sqrt{q(q - r_s)}/2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi, w)$, with $v = ct + \sqrt{q/r_s}\,r_*$ and $w = y + \sqrt{(q - r_s)/r_s}\,r_*$ both lengths, where $r_* = r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$. The circle of $w$ has any length $L$.

charts.name: Magnetic Charge

parameters.description: Radius of the horizon
Charge length; $p \ge r_s$, and $p = r_s$ is no charge. In units with $G = c = 1$ in four dimensions the mass is $M = (p + r_s)/4$ and the magnetic charge $P = \sqrt{p(p - r_s)}/2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi, y)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and the fifth coordinate $y$ a length, periodic with period $4\pi\sqrt{p(p - r_s)}$. The potential $A_\phi = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{p(p - r_s)}\,(1 - \cos\theta)$ vanishes on the half axis $\theta = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

metric_components.value: r\left(r + p - r_s\right)\sin^2\theta + \dfrac{p\,r\left(p - r_s\right)\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)^2}{r + p - r_s}

charts.name: Equal Charges

parameters.description: Difference of the radii of the two horizons, $\rho = (p \pm r_s)/2$

Sum of the radii of the two horizons; $p \ge r_s$, and $p = r_s$ is no charge. In units with $G = c = 1$ in four dimensions the mass is $M = p/2$ and the electric and magnetic charges are equal, $Q = P = \sqrt{(p^2 - r_s^2)/8}$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi, y)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\rho$ the areal radius, and the fifth coordinate $y$ a length, periodic with period $4\pi\sqrt{(p^2 - r_s^2)/2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(1 - \dfrac{p + r_s}{2\rho}\right)\left(1 - \dfrac{p - r_s}{2\rho}\right)c^2dt^2 + \dfrac{d\rho^2}{\left(1 - \dfrac{p + r_s}{2\rho}\right)\left(1 - \dfrac{p - r_s}{2\rho}\right)} + \rho^2\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right) + \left(dy - \dfrac{1}{\rho}\sqrt{\dfrac{p^2 - r_s^2}{2}}\,c\,dt + \sqrt{\dfrac{p^2 - r_s^2}{2}}\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)d\phi\right)^2

charts.name: Einstein Metric, Four Dimensions

parameters.description: Radius of the horizon

Charge length, $q = r_s\cosh^2\alpha$ for a boost of rapidity $\alpha$ along the circle; $q \ge r_s$, and $q = r_s$ is no charge. In units with $G = c = 1$ in four dimensions the mass is $M = (q + r_s)/4$ and the electric charge $Q = \sqrt{q(q - r_s)}/2$

charts.convention:
We use coordinates $(t, r, 	heta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components of the Einstein metric $g_{\mu
u}$ of four dimensions, where $ds_5^2 = e^{-4\varphi/\sqrt{3}}(dy + 2A_\mu dx^\mu)^2 + e^{2\varphi/\sqrt{3}}g_{\mu
u}dx^\mu dx^
u$, in the chart $x^0 = ct$. The magnetic hole has the same metric with $p$ in place of $q$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{r - r_s}{\sqrt{r\left(r + q - r_s\right)}}c^2dt^2 + \dfrac{\sqrt{r\left(r + q - r_s\right)}}{r - r_s}dr^2 + r\sqrt{r\left(r + q - r_s\right)}\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right)

charts.name: Einstein Metric, Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Radius of the horizon

Charge length, $q = r_s\cosh^2\alpha$ for a boost of rapidity $\alpha$ along the circle; $q \ge r_s$, and $q = r_s$ is no charge. In units with $G = c = 1$ in four dimensions the mass is $M = (q + r_s)/4$ and the electric charge $Q = \sqrt{q(q - r_s)}/2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the Einstein metric of four dimensions, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \sqrt{r(r + q - r_s)}/(r - r_s)$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{r - r_s}{\sqrt{r\left(r + q - r_s\right)}}dv^2 + 2\,dv\,dr + r\sqrt{r\left(r + q - r_s\right)}\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right)

spacetimes.name: Kaluza-Klein Monopole
spacetimes.description: A static vacuum solution of gravity in five dimensions, four of space and one of time, that Rafael Sorkin, and David Gross and Malcolm Perry, found in 1983: Euclidean Taub-NUT space with a time added. The fifth dimension is a circle that shrinks smoothly to a point at the centre, and seen from four dimensions the twist of that circle is the field of a magnetic monopole.
spacetimes.convention: The length $m$ is the monopole's only parameter. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.

related.text: The monopole's four dimensions of space are Taub-NUT continued to Euclidean signature, in its self dual case and with NUT parameter $2m$. Sorkin made the monopole by giving that space a time [sorkin1983, hawking1977].

Rolled up to four dimensions, the monopole is the extreme magnetic black hole of Kaluza and Klein's theory, whose scalar field is a dilaton coupled with strength $\sqrt{3}$ where string theory's has strength $1$ [duff1994].

Any number of monopoles stay at rest wherever they are put, as Majumdar and Papapetrou's extremal black holes do, with $1 + \sum_i 4m/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$ in place of $1 + 4m/r$ [hawking1977, ruback1986].
A second static vacuum solution of gravity in five dimensions. Its 3-spheres are round and surround a horizon, and the monopole's are squashed and close smoothly at the nut.
Another vacuum solution of five dimensions with one direction rolled into a circle. Seen from four dimensions it is Schwarzschild's black hole, where the monopole is a magnetic charge [gregory2012].

A rotating black hole in five dimensions. With equal spins in its two planes each surface around it is a squashed 3-sphere as well, its Hopf circles stretched by the rotation where the monopole's shrink [emparan2008].
A fifth dimension of infinite size, with gravity held near a wall by the curvature of anti-de Sitter space [randall1999b].
The monopole with a horizon around it, together with its electric and dyonic relatives. At $r_s = 0$ the magnetic hole is the monopole, with $p = 4m$ [horowitz2012].

Gibbons and Hawking's space with two centres and no constant in its potential; the monopole's four dimensions of space have one centre and the constant $1$. It has no circle of fixed size far away, and its boundary there is a 3-sphere with opposite points identified [gibbonshawking1979, eguchihanson1979].
The static pair of opposite magnetic charges in Einstein-Maxwell theory. Gross and Perry's monopole and antimonopole pair is its counterpart in Kaluza-Klein theory [grossperry1983, emparan2000].

charts.name: Gross-Perry

parameters.description: The monopole's one length: the fifth dimension has circumference $16\pi m$ far away

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi, x_5)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and the fifth coordinate $x_5$ a length, periodic with period $16\pi m$. The potential $A_\phi = 4m(1 - \cos\theta)$ vanishes on the half axis $\theta = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Hopf Angle

parameters.description: The monopole's one length: the fifth dimension has circumference $16\pi m$ far away

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi, \psi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and the angle $\psi = -\phi - x_5/4m$ periodic with period $4\pi$, so that $(\theta, \phi, \psi)$ are Euler angles on each 3-sphere of constant $t$ and $r$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Taub-NUT Radius

parameters.description: The monopole's one length: the fifth dimension has circumference $16\pi m$ far away

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi, \psi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, the radius $\rho = r + 2m$ of the Taub-NUT line element with NUT parameter $2m$, and the Euler angle $\psi$ periodic with period $4\pi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Kantowski-Sachs Cosmologies
spacetimes.description: The spatially homogeneous, anisotropic cosmologies outside Bianchi's classification. Every moment of time is a cylinder $\mathbb{R} \times S^2$, or $S^1 \times S^2$, whose length and whose spheres evolve separately, and the vacuum member is the region inside the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: The vacuum member of the family is the inside of Schwarzschild's horizon, where $r$ is a time [ellismaccallum1969, doran2008].
Every other spatially homogeneous cosmology. The Kantowski-Sachs group has four parameters, and none of Bianchi's groups sits inside it acting simply transitively [kantowski1966, ellismaccallum1969].
Peter Szekeres's dust cosmologies of 1975 hold the Kantowski-Sachs dust models in their second class, and in general have no Killing vector [szekeres1975, bonnor1977].
With its axis wrapped into a circle, the member with no matter is a polarised Gowdy spacetime on $S^2 \times S^1$ [obregon1998].
A regular black hole whose inside, where $r$ is a time, is a Kantowski-Sachs cosmology that bounces: its spheres shrink to a least radius $a$ and grow again [bronnikov2022].

charts.name: Comoving

parameters.description: Scale factor along $r$, the axis of the cylinder ($a > 0$), dimensionless
Radius of the spheres, a length ($b > 0$); $a$ and $b$ are independent

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ a cosmic time, $r$ a comoving length along the axis of the cylinder, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ angles on the spheres. The scale factor $a(t)$ is dimensionless and the radius $b(t)$ of the spheres is a length, both free functions of $t$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is the derivative along that chart time, $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Vacuum (Schwarzschild Interior)

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(T, r, \theta, \phi)$, where the time $T$ is the areal radius of the spheres, a length, and $r$ is $c$ times Schwarzschild's $t$, a length along the axis of the cylinder. In the comoving chart $a = \sqrt{r_s/T - 1}$, $b = T$, and $c\,dt = dT/a$.

charts.name: Dust, Parametric Time

parameters.description: Largest radius the spheres reach, at $\eta = 0$, a length
Dimensionless constant with $|\kappa| < \pi/2$; the model is symmetric in time about $\eta = 0$ where $\kappa = 0$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $\eta$ a dimensionless time and $r$ a comoving length along the axis of the cylinder. In the comoving chart $a = 1 + (\eta + \kappa)\tan\eta$, $b = b_0\cos^2\eta$, and $c\,dt = 2b_0\cos^2\eta\,d\eta$, so $ct = b_0\left(\eta + \sin\eta\cos\eta\right)$. The dust is at rest in the chart, with density $\rho = \dfrac{c^2}{8\pi G\,a\,b^2}$.

spacetimes.name: Kasner Anisotropic Vacuum Cosmology
spacetimes.description: An anisotropic vacuum cosmology that expands along some axes while contracting along another, with expansion exponents constrained by two algebraic relations. It is a key building block of the chaotic approach to cosmological singularities.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The expansion exponents obey $p_1 + p_2 + p_3 = 1$ and $p_1^2 + p_2^2 + p_3^2 = 1$, and every component assumes both conditions.

related.text: Kasner's metric is the vacuum solution of Bianchi type I, the type whose space is flat [ellismaccallum1969].
Bianchi type IX in vacuum, which runs through an endless sequence of Kasner epochs on its way to the singularity [misner1969, bkl1970].
The exponents $(1, 0, 0)$ make Kasner's spacetime flat, a wedge of Minkowski space in coordinates that expand along one axis.
Kasner's metric with $t$ traded for a radius is the static field of a line of mass, which Tullio Levi-Civita had found in 1919 [levicivita1919, maccallum2011].
Two plane waves colliding end in a singularity near which the metric is Kasner's, with exponents set by the incoming waves [yurtsever1988].

Kasner's universe with gravitational waves running round a torus. The flat Kasner universe is the Gowdy torus with $P = \tau$ and $Q = 0$ [ringstrom2010], and a polarised Gowdy universe approaches a Kasner universe of its own at each $\theta$ as it nears the singularity [berger1974].

Send the mass of Schwarzschild's black hole to infinity in coordinates that stay inside the horizon, and the limit is the Kasner universe with exponents $(-\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{2}{3})$. Robert Geroch gave it in 1969 as an example of a limit that depends on the coordinates, since in others the same family tends to Minkowski space [geroch1969].

Edward Kasner found this solution too. In 1921, the year of his anisotropic vacuum, he presented the product of two equal spheres as a solution with a cosmological constant, the positive signature form of Nariai's metric [kasner1925, kasner1921].

charts.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Expansion exponent along $x$, with $p_1 + p_2 + p_3 = 1$
Expansion exponent along $y$, with $p_1^2 + p_2^2 + p_3^2 = 1$
Expansion exponent along $z$; the two constraints leave one free exponent, and every solution but $(1,0,0)$ and its permutations has one exponent negative

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and evaluate the powers $t^{2p_i}$ with $t$ in a fixed unit of time, so they are dimensionless and the lengths sit in $x$, $y$, and $z$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

spacetimes.name: Kastor-Traschen Colliding Black Holes
spacetimes.description: Any number of charged black holes in a universe with a positive cosmological constant, the exact solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations David Kastor and Jennie Traschen found in 1993. Each hole has a charge equal to its mass, and the holes ride the expansion or the contraction of the universe, so holes that fall together merge.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. Each hole carries the mass parameter $m_i = GM_i/c^2$, a length, and a charge $Q_i$ of one common sign with $GQ_i^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4) = m_i^2$. The cosmological constant is $\Lambda = 3H^2/c^2$.

related.text: These holes with the cosmological constant switched off. At $H = 0$ the time drops out of the metric and the holes stand still [kastor1993].
One hole alone is the lukewarm charged black hole in de Sitter space, the one as hot as its cosmological horizon, in coordinates that ride the expansion [kastor1993, brill1994].
The universe the holes ride in. With every mass set to zero the metric is de Sitter space in its flat slicing [kastor1993].
A mass in an expanding universe filled with fluid, where the pressure piles up around the mass to keep the density even [kastor1993].

Two uncharged black holes at rest in a universe with no cosmological constant. Only their first moment is in closed form, and the collision that follows is known from computer simulations [brill1963, sperhake2015].

charts.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Hubble rate of the de Sitter background, a frequency with $3H^2/c^2 = \Lambda$, positive for holes moving apart and negative for holes falling together
Dimensionless potential of the holes, $V = \sum_i m_i/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$ for holes at the points $\mathbf{x}_i$, harmonic away from them; no component assumes it harmonic
Dimensionless, the potential of the holes with the cosmological time added, so that $\partial_\tau U = H$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, x, y, z)$, with $\tau$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths, and take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{24H^4\,U^8 - 8c^2\,H^2\,U^5\left(\partial_x^2 V + \partial_y^2 V + \partial_z^2 V\right) + 4c^4\,U^2\left(2\partial_x^2 V\,\partial_y^2 V + 2\partial_x^2 V\,\partial_z^2 V + 2\partial_y^2 V\,\partial_z^2 V + 4\left(\partial_x\partial_y V\right)^2 + 4\left(\partial_x\partial_z V\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_x^2 V\right)^2 + 4\left(\partial_y\partial_z V\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_y^2 V\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_z^2 V\right)^2\right) - 8c^4\,U\left(12\partial_x V\,\partial_x\partial_y V\,\partial_y V + 12\partial_x V\,\partial_x\partial_z V\,\partial_z V + 12\partial_y V\,\partial_y\partial_z V\,\partial_z V + 5\left(\partial_x V\right)^2\,\partial_x^2 V - \left(\partial_x V\right)^2\,\partial_y^2 V - \left(\partial_x V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V + 5\left(\partial_y V\right)^2\,\partial_y^2 V - \left(\partial_y V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V + 5\left(\partial_z V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V - \partial_x^2 V\left(\partial_y V\right)^2 - \partial_x^2 V\left(\partial_z V\right)^2 - \partial_y^2 V\left(\partial_z V\right)^2\right) + 56c^4\left(\left(\partial_x V\right)^2 + \left(\partial_y V\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z V\right)^2\right)^2}{c^4\,U^8}

charts.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: Hubble rate of the de Sitter background, a frequency with $3H^2/c^2 = \Lambda$, positive for holes moving apart and negative for holes falling together
Dimensionless potential of the holes, $V = \sum_i m_i/\sqrt{\rho^2 + (z - z_i)^2}$ for holes at the points $z = z_i$ of the axis, harmonic away from them; no component assumes it harmonic
Dimensionless, the potential of the holes with the cosmological time added, so that $\partial_\tau U = H$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $\tau$ carrying dimensions of time, $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, and every hole on the axis $\rho = 0$, and take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{24H^4\,U^8\,\rho^2 - 8c^2\,H^2\,U^5\,\rho\left(\rho\,\partial_\rho^2 V + \rho\,\partial_z^2 V + \partial_\rho V\right) + 4c^4\,U^2\left(2\rho^2\,\partial_\rho^2 V\,\partial_z^2 V + 2\rho\,\partial_\rho V\,\partial_\rho^2 V + 2\rho\,\partial_\rho V\,\partial_z^2 V + 4\rho^2\left(\partial_\rho\partial_z V\right)^2 + 3\rho^2\left(\partial_\rho^2 V\right)^2 + 3\rho^2\left(\partial_z^2 V\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_\rho V\right)^2\right) - 8c^4\,U\,\rho\left(12\rho\,\partial_\rho V\,\partial_\rho\partial_z V\,\partial_z V - \rho\,\partial_\rho^2 V\left(\partial_z V\right)^2 + 5\rho\left(\partial_\rho V\right)^2\,\partial_\rho^2 V - \rho\left(\partial_\rho V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V + 5\rho\left(\partial_z V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V - \partial_\rho V\left(\partial_z V\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\rho V\right)^3\right) + 56c^4\,\rho^2\left(\left(\partial_\rho V\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z V\right)^2\right)^2}{c^4\,U^8\,\rho^2}

charts.name: Isotropic

parameters.description: Hubble rate of the de Sitter background, a frequency with $3H^2/c^2 = \Lambda$, positive for holes moving apart and negative for holes falling together
Mass parameter of the single hole, $m = GM/c^2$, equal to its charge radius
Dimensionless, the potential of the hole with the cosmological time added; the areal radius is $rU$

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, r, \theta, \phi)$ centred on a single hole, with $\tau$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length, and take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Comoving

parameters.description: Hubble rate of the de Sitter background, a frequency with $3H^2/c^2 = \Lambda$, positive for holes moving apart and negative for holes falling together
Scale factor of the de Sitter background, dimensionless
Dimensionless potential of the holes, $V = \sum_i m_i/|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_i|$ for holes at the points $\mathbf{x}_i$, harmonic away from them; no component assumes it harmonic
Dimensionless, the potential of the holes diluted by the scale factor and added to one; $a\Omega$ is the $U$ of the Cartesian chart

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving lengths, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{24H^4\,a^8\,\Omega^8 - 8c^2\,H^2\,a^5\,\Omega^5\left(\partial_x^2 V + \partial_y^2 V + \partial_z^2 V\right) + 4c^4\,a^2\,\Omega^2\left(2\partial_x^2 V\,\partial_y^2 V + 2\partial_x^2 V\,\partial_z^2 V + 2\partial_y^2 V\,\partial_z^2 V + 4\left(\partial_x\partial_y V\right)^2 + 4\left(\partial_x\partial_z V\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_x^2 V\right)^2 + 4\left(\partial_y\partial_z V\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_y^2 V\right)^2 + 3\left(\partial_z^2 V\right)^2\right) - 8c^4\,a\,\Omega\left(12\partial_x V\,\partial_x\partial_y V\,\partial_y V + 12\partial_x V\,\partial_x\partial_z V\,\partial_z V + 12\partial_y V\,\partial_y\partial_z V\,\partial_z V + 5\left(\partial_x V\right)^2\,\partial_x^2 V - \left(\partial_x V\right)^2\,\partial_y^2 V - \left(\partial_x V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V + 5\left(\partial_y V\right)^2\,\partial_y^2 V - \left(\partial_y V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V + 5\left(\partial_z V\right)^2\,\partial_z^2 V - \partial_x^2 V\left(\partial_y V\right)^2 - \partial_x^2 V\left(\partial_z V\right)^2 - \partial_y^2 V\left(\partial_z V\right)^2\right) + 56c^4\left(\left(\partial_x V\right)^2 + \left(\partial_y V\right)^2 + \left(\partial_z V\right)^2\right)^2}{c^4\,a^8\,\Omega^8}

spacetimes.name: Kerr Rotating Black Hole
spacetimes.description: The exact vacuum solution for a rotating, uncharged black hole, characterized by mass and angular momentum. It features an ergosphere, frame dragging, and a ring singularity, and describes essentially all astrophysical black holes.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the two parameters are the mass $M$ and the spin per unit mass $a = J/(Mc)$, which carries dimensions of length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: Kerr's black hole with the spin switched off, $a = 0$. The horizon is a round sphere again and the ergosphere is gone.
Kerr's black hole given an electric charge to carry as it spins. At $r_Q = 0$ it is Kerr's metric.
A rotating black hole in three dimensions, with an outer and an inner horizon like Kerr's and the same curvature at every point [banados1992, banados1993].
A rotating wormhole with an ergoregion and no horizon. Its ergoregion is a tube round the equator of the throat, and the Penrose process draws energy from it as it does from Kerr's [teo1998].
Between the outer and inner horizons $r$ is a time, and with $t$ wrapped into a circle the region is a Gowdy spacetime on $S^2 \times S^1$ [obregon1998, garfinkle1999].

Kerr's metric with $\sqrt{r^2 + \ell^2}$ written for the Boyer-Lindquist radius and $dr$ left alone is the rotating black bounce of Mazza, Franzin, and Liberati, a regular black hole or a wormhole depending on $\ell$ [mazza2021].
Kerr's black hole in a universe with a cosmological constant of either sign. At $\Lambda = 0$ Carter's metric is Kerr's [carter1968separable].
Kerr's black hole in more than four dimensions, with a spin for every independent plane of rotation. From six dimensions up a hole turning in one plane keeps its horizon at every spin [myers1986].
Kerr spinning as fast as it can, seen from just outside the horizon. The region there is a throat without end, with four symmetries where Kerr has two [bardeen1999].

The field outside a slowly rotating star, to second order in its spin. The star's quadrupole moment is free, and at Kerr's value, $Q = J^2/M$, the field is Kerr's metric to that order [hartlethorne1968].

Kerr's black hole is a Malament-Hogarth spacetime. An observer falling to the inner horizon has by then received every signal a computer orbiting outside will ever send, however long it runs [etesi2002].

The charged black hole, which has an inner horizon as Kerr's does and spherical symmetry besides. Eric Poisson and Werner Israel took it in 1989 as a simple spherical model of the inside of a spinning hole, and found the mass within the inner horizon growing without bound [poisson1989, poisson1990].
Schwarzschild's metric with a twist $l$ where Kerr's has a spin $a$. Jerzy Plebański and Marek Demiański's family of 1976 holds both parameters at once [plebanski1976, griffiths2005].

The static field of a rod, which deforms Schwarzschild's metric by a quadrupole. Akira Tomimatsu and Humitaka Sato found a spinning vacuum solution in 1972 that is Kerr's metric at one value of its angular momentum and a Zipoy-Voorhees metric at none [tomimatsu1972, kodamahikida2003].

The static black hole of $D$ dimensions. Robert Myers and Malcolm Perry found its spinning family in 1986, the counterparts of Kerr's metric in higher dimensions, where a black hole can turn in several planes at once [myers1986, emparan2008].

A black hole with an acceleration where Kerr's has a spin. Jerzy Plebański and Marek Demiański put both into one family in 1976, and the spinning C-metric is Kerr's metric when the acceleration vanishes [plebanski1976, griffiths2005].

The throat of an extremal charged black hole, AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$. James Bardeen and Gary Horowitz found in 1999 that the limit toward the horizon of an extreme Kerr black hole is its vacuum counterpart, with a timelike boundary at infinity as well [bardeen1999].

Kerr's metric with the mass taken out, $M = 0$, which is flat, in spheroidal coordinates built on a ring of radius $a$. Gary Gibbons and Mikhail Volkov pointed out in 2017 that the ring stays and joins two flat regions, so at $M = 0$ Kerr's spacetime is Minkowski space only locally [gibbons2017].

The shock wave of a black hole boosted to the speed of light. Valeria Ferrari and Paolo Pendenza boosted Kerr's along its axis in 1990, and took the limit to be the field of massless particles on a ring of radius $a$ [ferrari1990].

A star that shines. Prahlad Vaidya and L. K. Patel found a radiating Kerr metric in 1973, a field of flowing radiation with Kerr's symmetry that is Kerr's metric when the radiation is switched off [vaidya1973].

Two impulsive plane waves colliding. With their polarisations out of line the collision is Yavuz Nutku and Mustafa Halil's solution, which Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar and Valeria Ferrari derived in 1984 from the simplest solution of an equation of Ernst's type, as Kerr's metric is derived [chandrasekhar1984ferrari, nutku1977].

Schwarzschild's black hole with a cosmic string through it. Ruth Gregory, David Kubizňák, and Danielle Wills put the string through a Kerr black hole in 2013 and found its effect conical in a frame turning with the hole [gregory2013].

A charged spherical hole crossed by two streams of radiation, the model Eric Poisson and Werner Israel built in 1989 for the inside of a rotating one. Its mass function grows without limit at the inner horizon [poisson1989].
Kerr's black hole given a NUT parameter $l$ beside its spin. At $l = 0$ it is Kerr's metric, and for $|l| > |a|$ the ring singularity is gone [griffiths2005].

Two Kerr black holes on one axis, built by Dietrich Kramer and Gernot Neugebauer in 1980. The repulsion between the spins does not balance the attraction, and a strut on the axis between the holes holds them apart [kramer1980, neugebauer2009].
A cloud of rotating dust whose field far away is Kerr's frame dragging term alone: angular momentum with no mass [bonnor1977cloud, bratek2007].
A static magnet made from Kerr's metric. Bonnor's rule trades the twist of the spinning hole for a magnetic potential and turns $a^2$ into $-b^2$ [bonnor2002, davidson1994].
Kerr's hole with a rigidly rotating perfect fluid laid over it. Wahlquist's family in Mars's chart is Kerr's metric at $\beta = 0$, $\mu_0 = 0$, and $a_1 = 0$ [mars2001].

charts.name: Kerr (Boyer-Lindquist)

parameters.description: Mass of the black hole
Spin per unit mass, $a = J/(Mc)$ with $J$ the angular momentum, carrying dimensions of length; a horizon exists only for $a \le GM/c^2$
Newton's constant, kept explicit along with $c$, so that the Schwarzschild radius appears throughout as $2GM/c^2$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates of Robert Boyer and Richard Lindquist, $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. The horizons are at $r_\pm = GM/c^2 \pm \sqrt{G^2M^2/c^4 - a^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(1 - \dfrac{2GMr}{c^2\left(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta\right)}\right)c^2 dt^2 - \dfrac{4GMar\sin^2\theta}{c^2\left(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta\right)}c\,dt\,d\phi + \dfrac{r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta}{r^2 + a^2 - \dfrac{2GMr}{c^2}}dr^2 + \left(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta\right)d\theta^2 + \left(r^2 + a^2 + \dfrac{2GMa^2r\sin^2\theta}{c^2\left(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta\right)}\right)\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2

spacetimes.name: Kerr-de Sitter and Kerr-anti-de Sitter Black Holes
spacetimes.description: The rotating black hole in a universe with a cosmological constant of either sign, which Brandon Carter found in 1968 among the spacetimes whose geodesic equations separate. With $\Lambda > 0$ an inner horizon, an event horizon, and a cosmological horizon surround the ring singularity, and with $\Lambda < 0$ its boundary is a rotating Einstein universe.
spacetimes.convention: The mass enters as the length $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the rotation parameter $a$ is a length, and the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ takes either sign, with $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2$ for Kerr-anti-de Sitter. The horizons are the real roots of $\Delta_r$, $r_- < r_+$ and, for $\Lambda > 0$, $r_c$ beyond them and $r_n$ at negative values, with surface gravities $\kappa_-$, $\kappa_+$, $\kappa_c$, and $\kappa_n$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.

related.text: Carter's black hole with the cosmological constant switched off. At $\Lambda = 0$ the cosmological horizon is gone and $\Xi = \Delta_\theta = 1$.
Kerr-de Sitter with the spin switched off, $a = 0$ and $\Lambda > 0$. Kottler's two horizons are what is left of $r_+$ and $r_c$.
Kerr-anti-de Sitter with the spin switched off, $a = 0$ and $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2$. Its boundary is an Einstein universe at rest.
Kerr's black hole with a charge where this one has a cosmological constant. Both sit in the family Carter found by asking the Hamilton-Jacobi equation to separate [carter1968separable].
Kerr-de Sitter with the mass taken out, $r_s = 0$ and $\Lambda > 0$. The rotation parameter $a$ is left over as a choice of spheroidal coordinates, which Akcay and Matzner untwist [akcay2011].
Kerr-anti-de Sitter with the mass taken out, $r_s = 0$ and $\Lambda < 0$, which is anti-de Sitter space in unusual coordinates [henneaux1985].

The rotating black hole of anti-de Sitter space in three dimensions. Hawking, Hunter, and Taylor-Robinson set its boundary, a rotating Einstein universe as well, beside this one's [hawking1999rotation].
The black hole of de Sitter space with a charge where this one has a spin. Its horizons are arranged the same way, an inner one, an outer one, and a cosmological one [lake2015].
A black hole with an acceleration where this one has a spin. Plebański and Demiański put both, and the cosmological constant, into one family of solutions [kamran2009, plebanski1976].
Kerr's black hole with a NUT parameter where this one has a cosmological constant. Carter's separable family holds both [carter1968separable, bini2003].
Carter's hole with its cosmological constant traded for a rotating fluid whose $\mu + 3p$ is constant. Where the fluid's density and pressure cancel, Wahlquist's family is Kerr-de Sitter [mars2001].

charts.name: Boyer-Lindquist
domains: \Delta_r = 0 \;\text{(the event horizon } r_+ \text{ and, for } \Lambda > 0 \text{, the cosmological horizon } r_c\text{)}

parameters.description: Mass parameter as a length, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$; the mass measured against the de Sitter or anti-de Sitter background is $M/\Xi^2$
Rotation parameter, a length; the angular momentum is $J = aMc/\Xi^2$, and $a = 0$ is Kottler's metric
Cosmological constant, an inverse length squared, of either sign: Kerr-de Sitter for $\Lambda > 0$, Kerr for $\Lambda = 0$, and Kerr-anti-de Sitter for $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2 < 0$, where $|a| < \ell$
Keeps the axis free of a conical singularity with the azimuthal angle periodic in $2\pi$
Vanishes on the ring singularity, $r = 0$ on the equator
A quartic in $r$ whose real roots are the horizons: $r_- < r_+$ for $\Lambda \le 0$, and $r_- < r_+ < r_c$ with a fourth root at negative $r$ for $\Lambda > 0$
Equal to $\Xi$ on the axis and to $1$ on the equator

charts.convention: We use Carter's metric in the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Hawking, Hunter, and Taylor-Robinson, which are Boyer and Lindquist's at $\Lambda = 0$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$, and write $\Xi$, $\rho$, $\Delta_r$, and $\Delta_\theta$ as the parameters define them. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \Phi)$ with $\Phi = \phi - a\Lambda ct/3$, the angle of Henneaux and Teitelboim's frame that does not rotate as $r \to \infty$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and write $\Xi$, $\rho$, $\Delta_r$, and $\Delta_\theta$ as the parameters define them. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

parameters.description: Mass parameter as a length, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$; the mass measured against the de Sitter or anti-de Sitter background is $M/\Xi^2$

charts.name: Kerr-Schild

parameters.description: Mass parameter as a length, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$; the mass measured against the de Sitter or anti-de Sitter background is $M/\Xi^2$
Rotation parameter, a length; the angular momentum is $J = aMc/\Xi^2$, and $a = 0$ is Kottler's metric
Cosmological constant, an inverse length squared, of either sign: Kerr-de Sitter for $\Lambda > 0$, Kerr for $\Lambda = 0$, and Kerr-anti-de Sitter for $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2 < 0$, where $|a| < \ell$
Keeps the axis free of a conical singularity with the azimuthal angle periodic in $2\pi$
Vanishes on the ring singularity, $r = 0$ on the equator
A quartic in $r$ whose real roots are the horizons: $r_- < r_+$ for $\Lambda \le 0$, and $r_- < r_+ < r_c$ with a fourth root at negative $r$ for $\Lambda > 0$
Equal to $\Xi$ on the axis and to $1$ on the equator

charts.convention: We use the Kerr-Schild coordinates $(\tau, r, \theta, \psi)$ of Gibbons, Lü, Page, and Pope, with $c\,d\tau = c\,dt + r_s r\,dr/((1 - \Lambda r^2/3)\Delta_r)$ and $d\psi = d\phi - (a\Lambda/3)\,c\,dt + a r_s r\,dr/((r^2 + a^2)\Delta_r)$, and write $\Xi$, $\rho$, $\Delta_r$, and $\Delta_\theta$ as the parameters define them. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{\Delta_\theta}{\Xi}\left(1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}\right)c^2\,d\tau^2 + \dfrac{\rho^2}{\left(1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}\right)\left(r^2 + a^2\right)}dr^2 + \dfrac{\rho^2}{\Delta_\theta}d\theta^2 + \dfrac{r^2 + a^2}{\Xi}\sin^2\theta\,d\psi^2 + \dfrac{r_s r}{\rho^2}\left(\dfrac{\Delta_\theta}{\Xi}c\,d\tau + \dfrac{\rho^2}{\left(1 - \dfrac{\Lambda r^2}{3}\right)\left(r^2 + a^2\right)}dr - \dfrac{a\sin^2\theta}{\Xi}d\psi\right)^2

spacetimes.name: Kerr-Newman Charged Rotating Black Hole
spacetimes.description: The most general stationary black hole solution, carrying mass, angular momentum, and electric charge. It unifies the Kerr and Reissner-Nordström metrics into a single electrovacuum spacetime.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the parameters are the mass $M$, the spin per unit mass $a = J/(Mc)$, which carries dimensions of length, and the charge radius $r_Q$, fixed by $r_Q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0 c^4)$ from the total electric charge $Q$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

related.text: Kerr-Newman with neither spin nor charge, $a = 0$ and $r_Q = 0$, where only the mass is left.
Kerr-Newman with the charge set to zero, $r_Q = 0$. Ezra Newman's group reached the charged metric by the complex shift that carries Schwarzschild's metric to Kerr's [newman1965janis, newman1965kn].
Kerr-Newman with the spin switched off, $a = 0$, a charged black hole that does not turn.
Kerr's black hole with a cosmological constant where this one has a charge. Carter found both in one family by asking the Hamilton-Jacobi equation to separate [carter1968separable].
The throat of the extreme hole with the charge switched off. With charge the throat slides toward the Bertotti-Robinson universe [bardeen1999].

Kerr-Newman is a Malament-Hogarth spacetime, as Gábor Etesi and István Németi noted in 2002 when they set a computer in orbit around Kerr's black hole and sent an observer in to the inner horizon [etesi2002].

The charged black hole of low energy string theory. Ashoke Sen set it spinning in 1992, which makes his solution string theory's counterpart of Kerr-Newman, with mass, charge, and angular momentum [sen1992].
With charge equal to mass, Kerr and Newman's metric is one spinning source of Israel, Wilson, and Perjés's fields, which hold any number of such sources in balance [hartle1972, perjes1971].
Kerr's black hole with a NUT parameter where this one has a charge. Marek Demiański and Ezra Newman's electrovacuum solutions of 1966 carry both, and a magnetic charge too [manko2006].

charts.name: Kerr-Newman (Boyer-Lindquist)

parameters.description: Mass of the black hole
Spin per unit mass, $a = J/(Mc)$ with $J$ the angular momentum, carrying dimensions of length
Newton's constant, kept explicit along with $c$, so that the Schwarzschild radius appears throughout as $2GM/c^2$
Charge radius, $r_Q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0 c^4)$ with $Q$ the total electric charge, carrying dimensions of length; a horizon exists only for $a^2 + r_Q^2 \le G^2M^2/c^4$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates of Robert Boyer and Richard Lindquist, $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time. The horizons are at $r_\pm = GM/c^2 \pm \sqrt{G^2M^2/c^4 - a^2 - r_Q^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(1 - \dfrac{\dfrac{2GMr}{c^2} - r_Q^2}{r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta}\right)c^2 dt^2 - \dfrac{2a\sin^2\theta\left(\dfrac{2GMr}{c^2} - r_Q^2\right)}{r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta}c\,dt\,d\phi + \dfrac{r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta}{r^2 + a^2 - \dfrac{2GMr}{c^2} + r_Q^2}dr^2 + \left(r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta\right)d\theta^2 + \left(r^2 + a^2 + \dfrac{a^2\sin^2\theta\left(\dfrac{2GMr}{c^2} - r_Q^2\right)}{r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta}\right)\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2

spacetimes.name: Kerr-Taub-NUT Black Hole
spacetimes.description: Kerr's rotating black hole with a NUT parameter, the vacuum solution Marek Demiański and Ezra Newman found in 1966. It is Kerr's metric at $l = 0$ and the Taub-NUT metric at $a = 0$, it carries Misner strings along its axis, and for $|l| > |a|$ it has no curvature singularity.
spacetimes.convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit; the mass enters as the length $m = GM/c^2$, and the rotation parameter $a$ and the NUT parameter $l$ are lengths.

related.text: Kerr-Taub-NUT with the twist taken out, $l = 0$. The Misner strings go with it, and the ring singularity settles back on the equator.
Kerr-Taub-NUT with the spin switched off, $a = 0$ [bini2003].
Both the spin and the twist switched off, $a = l = 0$.
Kerr's black hole with an electric charge where this one has a twist. Demiański and Newman's solutions of 1966 include the black hole that carries both [manko2006].
Kerr's black hole with a cosmological constant where this one has a twist. Both belong to the family Carter found by asking the Hamilton-Jacobi equation to separate [carter1968separable, bini2003].

A black hole with an acceleration where this one has a twist. Plebański and Demiański's family of 1976 holds spin, twist, and acceleration together, and in Jerry Griffiths and Jiří Podolský's form of it Kerr-Taub-NUT is what is left when the acceleration vanishes [plebanski1976, griffiths2005].

The Kerr-NUT metric with a rigidly rotating perfect fluid laid over it in the same region, which is how Wahlquist described his solution. With the fluid taken away his family is the Kerr-NUT vacuum [wahlquist1968, mars2001].

charts.name: Boyer-Lindquist

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, a length
Rotation parameter, a length; at $a = 0$ the metric is the Taub-NUT metric
NUT parameter, a length, the gravitomagnetic monopole moment; at $l = 0$ the metric is Kerr's
Vanishes only on the ring $r = 0$, $\cos\theta = -l/a$, which exists for $|l| \le |a|$
Its roots are the horizons, which exist for $a^2 \le m^2 + l^2$
Equal to $-2l$ on the northern half of the axis and to $2l$ on the southern half, each a Misner string

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Boyer and Lindquist's kind, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and a Misner string on each half of the axis, and write $\Sigma$, $\Delta$, and $\chi$ as the parameters define them. The horizons are at $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 + l^2 - a^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{48\left(\left(m^2 - l^2\right)\left(r^6 - 15r^4\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^2 + 15r^2\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^4 - \left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^6\right) + 4mlr\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)\left(3r^4 - 10r^2\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^2 + 3\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^4\right)\right)}{\Sigma^6}

charts.name: One Misner String

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, a length
Rotation parameter, a length; at $a = 0$ the metric is the Taub-NUT metric
NUT parameter, a length, the gravitomagnetic monopole moment; at $l = 0$ the metric is Kerr's
Vanishes only on the ring $r = 0$, $\cos\theta = -l/a$, which exists for $|l| \le |a|$
Its roots are the horizons, which exist for $a^2 \le m^2 + l^2$
Vanishes on the northern half of the axis and is $4l$ on the southern half, the one Misner string

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t_N, r, \theta, \phi)$ with $t_N = t + 2l\phi/c$, the time in which the northern half of the axis is regular and one Misner string lies along $\theta = \pi$, and write $\Sigma$, $\Delta$, and $\chi$ as the parameters define them. The horizons are at $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 + l^2 - a^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct_N$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t_N}$ means $d(ct_N)/d\lambda$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{48\left(\left(m^2 - l^2\right)\left(r^6 - 15r^4\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^2 + 15r^2\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^4 - \left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^6\right) + 4mlr\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)\left(3r^4 - 10r^2\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^2 + 3\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^4\right)\right)}{\Sigma^6}

The horizons are at $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 + l^2 - a^2}$.

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, a length
Rotation parameter, a length; at $a = 0$ the metric is the Taub-NUT metric

The horizons are at $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 + l^2 - a^2}$.
charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{48\left(\left(m^2 - l^2\right)\left(r^6 - 15r^4\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^2 + 15r^2\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^4 - \left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^6\right) + 4mlr\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)\left(3r^4 - 10r^2\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^2 + 3\left(l + a\cos\theta\right)^4\right)\right)}{\Sigma^6}

charts.name: Plebański-Demiański
domains: Q = 0 \;\text{(the horizons } q_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 + l^2 - a^2}\text{)}

parameters.description: Geometric mass, $m = GM/c^2$, a length
Rotation parameter, a length; at $a = 0$ the metric is the Taub-NUT metric
NUT parameter, a length, the gravitomagnetic monopole moment; at $l = 0$ the metric is Kerr's
Its roots are the horizons, which exist for $a^2 \le m^2 + l^2$
Vanishes on the axis, $p = l \pm a$

charts.convention: We use the coordinates $(\tau, q, p, \sigma)$ of Plebański and Demiański, with $q = r$, $p = l + a\cos\theta$, $\sigma = -\phi/a$, and $\tau = ct - (a^2 + l^2)\phi/a$ a length that stands as the time, and write $Q$ and $P$ as the parameters define them. The horizons are at $q_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 + l^2 - a^2}$.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{Q}{p^2 + q^2}\left(d\tau - p^2\,d\sigma\right)^2 + \dfrac{p^2 + q^2}{Q}dq^2 + \dfrac{p^2 + q^2}{P}dp^2 + \dfrac{P}{p^2 + q^2}\left(d\tau + q^2\,d\sigma\right)^2

spacetimes.name: Khan-Penrose Colliding Plane Waves
spacetimes.description: Two impulsive plane gravitational waves colliding head on in flat space. Each focuses the other, and the vacuum where both have passed ends in a spacelike curvature singularity.
spacetimes.convention: No coordinate carries dimensions of time, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

related.text: Near the singularity made by the collision the metric approaches a Kasner solution whose exponents vary along the singularity [yurtsever1988].
Each incoming wave alone is a plane wave of this family. Roger Penrose showed in 1965 how strongly such a wave focuses light [penrose1965plane].
The calm before the collision. Spacetime is flat ahead of both waves, and flat again behind either one alone [frauendiener2014].

The same collision with light for the waves. Bell and Szekeres's two electromagnetic shock waves meet in the same four regions and focus each other onto a Killing-Cauchy horizon, with the curvature bounded [bell1974, griffiths1991].

The rotating black hole. Chandrasekhar and Ferrari wrote in 1984 that Nutku and Halil's collision, which is Khan and Penrose's with the polarisations out of line, occupies the same place among spacetimes with two spacelike Killing vectors "as the Kerr solution does" among those with one timelike and one spacelike [chandrasekhar1984ferrari].

Peter Szekeres's dust cosmologies of 1975 [szekeres1975]. Five years earlier he had given a solution for part of a collision of gravitational waves, and in 1972 the general solution for two plane waves that are linearly polarised [szekeres1970, szekeres1972].

An impulsive wave whose strength falls off with distance from one massless particle at its centre. Two of them meeting head on close a trapped surface around the collision, as Penrose found in 1974, so a black hole forms [eardley2002].

charts.name: Double Null

parameters.description: Focal length of each wave, in the frame where the two are equal: behind one wave alone the null rays across its front meet at $u = 1$ or $v = 1$.

charts.convention: We use null coordinates $(u, v, x, y)$ where both waves have passed, $u$ and $v$ dimensionless and $x$ and $y$ lengths across the wave fronts. Ahead of one wave or both, where $u < 0$ or $v < 0$, the metric is this one with $u$ or $v$ set to zero.
charts.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{2L^2\left(1 - u^2 - v^2\right)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2}\left(uv + \sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2}\right)^2}du\,dv + \left(1 - u^2 - v^2\right)\dfrac{1 + u\sqrt{1 - v^2} + v\sqrt{1 - u^2}}{1 - u\sqrt{1 - v^2} - v\sqrt{1 - u^2}}dx^2 + \left(1 - u^2 - v^2\right)\dfrac{1 - u\sqrt{1 - v^2} - v\sqrt{1 - u^2}}{1 + u\sqrt{1 - v^2} + v\sqrt{1 - u^2}}dy^2

metric_components.value: -\dfrac{L^2\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} - u\,v\right)\sqrt{1 - u^2 - v^2}}{\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} + u\,v\right)\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2}}
-\dfrac{L^2\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} - u\,v\right)\sqrt{1 - u^2 - v^2}}{\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} + u\,v\right)\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2}}
\dfrac{\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} + u\,v\right)\left(1 + u\sqrt{1 - v^2} + v\sqrt{1 - u^2}\right)^2}{\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} - u\,v}
\dfrac{\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} + u\,v\right)\left(1 - u\sqrt{1 - v^2} - v\sqrt{1 - u^2}\right)^2}{\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} - u\,v}

charts.kretschmann: K = \dfrac{3\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} - u\,v\right)^4 + 63\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} + u\,v\right)^4 - 18\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} - u\,v\right)^2\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} + u\,v\right)^2}{L^4\left(\sqrt{1 - u^2}\sqrt{1 - v^2} - u\,v\right)^4\left(1 - u^2 - v^2\right)^3}

charts.name: Cosmological

parameters.description: Focal length of each wave, in the frame where the two are equal: behind one wave alone the null rays across its front meet at $u = 1$ or $v = 1$.

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(\tau, \sigma, x, y)$ where both waves have passed, with $\tau = \arcsin u + \arcsin v$ and $\sigma = \arcsin u - \arcsin v$ dimensionless, and $x$ and $y$ lengths across the wave fronts.

spacetimes.name: Kiselev Black Hole
spacetimes.description: Schwarzschild's black hole with one more term in its metric, a power of the radius that stands for matter around the hole whose pressure, averaged over directions, is a fixed multiple of its energy density. Valery Kiselev wrote it down in 2003 as a black hole surrounded by quintessence, and Matt Visser showed in 2020 that the matter is neither a perfect fluid nor quintessence.
spacetimes.convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and $r_q$ is a length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.

related.text: Kiselev's black hole at $w = 0$, where the added term is $r_q/r$ and the metric is Schwarzschild's with radius $r_s + r_q$. Dust at rest adds mass and nothing else [kiselev2003].
Kiselev's black hole at $w = -1$, where the added term is $r^2/r_q^2$: Kottler's metric with $\Lambda = 3/r_q^2$, the matter a cosmological constant [kiselev2003].

At $w = 1/3$ the added term goes as $1/r^2$, and with its sign reversed the metric is Reissner-Nordström's. Visser pointed to this case: the matter is then an electric field, which is no perfect fluid [kiselev2003, visser2020].

At $w = -1/3$ the added term, which Visser writes $K/r^{3w+1}$, is a constant, and $f = 1 - K - r_s/r$ is the metric outside a global monopole with solid angle deficit $K$. Kiselev noted the "angle defect" of the spheres himself [kiselev2003, visser2020, barriola1989].

Kiselev's metric at $w = -1$ with no black hole, $r_s = 0$ and $\Lambda = 3/r_q^2$. Kiselev set his matter at $w = -2/3$ beside it: near the horizon the two metrics agree up to a constant conformal factor [kiselev2003].
Kiselev's matter alone at $w = -2/3$ is conformal to the part $\tau + \rho > 0$ of Minkowski space, with the factor $4r_q^2/(\tau + \rho)^2$ [kiselev2003].

charts.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Normalisation length of the surrounding matter
State parameter, the ratio of the pressure averaged over directions to the energy density
Kiselev's term in the metric function

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$. We write Kiselev's term as $h = (r_q/r)^{3w + 1}$.

charts.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Normalisation length of the surrounding matter
State parameter, the ratio of the pressure averaged over directions to the energy density
Kiselev's term in the metric function

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r - h\right)^{-1}$, $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$, and $h = (r_q/r)^{3w + 1}$ is Kiselev's term.

charts.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Normalisation length of the surrounding matter
State parameter, the ratio of the pressure averaged over directions to the energy density
Kiselev's term in the metric function

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/r - h\right)^{-1}$, $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$, and $h = (r_q/r)^{3w + 1}$ is Kiselev's term.

charts.name: Static, Linear Term

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$
Normalisation length of the surrounding matter

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. The state parameter is $w = -2/3$, and for $r_q > 4r_s$ the horizons are $r_\pm = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(r_q \pm \sqrt{r_q^2 - 4r_qr_s}\right)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

charts.name: Free Matter, Hyperbolic

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter

charts.convention: We use dimensionless coordinates $(\eta, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $\eta = ct/2r_q$ and $\chi = -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1 - r/r_q)$ in the static coordinates at $w = -2/3$ and $r_s = 0$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

charts.name: Free Matter, Conformally Flat

parameters.description: Normalisation length of the surrounding matter

charts.convention: We use dimensionless coordinates $(\tau, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $\tau = e^{\eta}\cosh\chi$ and $\rho = e^{\eta}\sinh\chi$ in the hyperbolic coordinates $\eta$ and $\chi$, so the areal radius is $r = 2r_q\rho/(\tau + \rho)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

spacetimes.name: Krasnikov Tube
spacetimes.description: A tube of modified spacetime laid down along the path of an outbound ship, flat inside but with its light cones tipped so far open that the trip home can be superluminal. The outbound leg is no faster than light, yet the round trip can be made arbitrarily short by clocks left at home, and holding the tube open takes negative energy density.

related.text: The warp bubble, whose pilot is cut off from the bubble wall and can neither raise it nor steer it [alcubierre1994, everett1997].

A warp bubble with a roomy pocket folded inside it. Krasnikov called the fold Van Den Broeck's trick, and with a pocket of his own brought the exotic matter of a shortcut down to about a milligram [krasnikov2003].
A wormhole made into a time machine by putting its two mouths out of step. Two Krasnikov tubes that do not overlap make one too, as Allen Everett and Thomas Roman showed in 1997 [everett1997].
Spacetime is flat outside the tube and flat again inside it, where the light cones are opened out. All of the curvature is in the tube's thin wall [everett1997].

charts.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: Shape function of the tube, dimensionless, an arbitrary function of $t$, $x$ and $r$ and not of $\phi$. It is $1$ wherever the tube is not, and there the line element is Minkowski in cylindrical coordinates; deep inside the tube it is a constant below $1$, Krasnikov's $-1 + \delta$ with $\delta$ small and positive, and the wall is wherever it falls between. Every derivative of $k$ is therefore supported on the wall alone and the spacetime is flat everywhere else. Krasnikov assembles his own $k$ out of smoothed step functions: one closes the tube off at a radius, one holds it inside the future light cone of the departure so that nothing is ever built ahead of the ship, and a pair opens it between the start of the journey and its end. No component needs that choice, and every component is an identity for an arbitrary $k$. The one thing they do need is $k > -1$, since $1 + k$ divides every one of them and the metric degenerates where it vanishes.

charts.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, r, \phi)$, cylindrical about the axis along which the tube is laid: $t$ carries dimensions of time, $x$ is length measured along the axis, $r$ is distance from the axis, and $\phi$ is the angle around it. The shape function $k$ is a dimensionless function of $t$, $x$, and $r$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, where $\partial_t = c^{-1}\partial/\partial t$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
